$$\left(1 + \frac{1}{k}\right)^3 \le \left(1 + \frac{1}{4}\right)^3 = \left(\frac{5}{4}\right)^3
= \frac{125}{64} = 1.953125 < 2 \tag{A1}$$

and hence $2k^3 > (k+1)^3$ strictly. Combining, $2^{k+1} > 2k^3 > (k+1)^3$, which is
$P(k+1)$ (AG). The condition $k \ge 4$ is used exactly once, at the point where
$\left(1 + \frac{1}{k}\right)^3$ is bounded above by its value at $k = 4$ (R1).

(c) Take $n = 10$ as the base case. By part (a), $2^{10} = 1024 > 1000 = 10^3$, so $P(10)$
holds (A1). By part (b) the implication $P(k) \Rightarrow P(k+1)$ holds for every $k \ge 4$,
and in particular for every $k \ge 10$ (M1). By the principle of mathematical induction
$P(n)$ is true for all integers $n \ge 10$ (A1).

(d) From (c), every $n \ge 10$ satisfies $P(n)$. From (a), among $1 \le n \le 10$ only
$n = 1$ and $n = 10$ do (A1). Therefore the complete set is

$$\{n \in \mathbb{Z}^{+} : 2^n > n^3\} = \{1\} \cup \{n \in \mathbb{Z}^{+} : n \ge 10\} \tag{A1}$$

The value $n = 1$ is isolated: $P(1)$ and $P(2)$ differ in truth value and no induction
connects them, so the answer cannot be written as a single inequality $n \ge N$ (R1). A
candidate who answers $n \ge 10$ has missed one value; a candidate who answers $n \ge 4$ has
used the threshold of the *step* rather than the threshold of the *statement* and is wrong at
$n = 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9$.
questions.explanation:
The item looks like a routine induction and is not one, because the induction has two
thresholds and the candidate has to find both.

The first threshold belongs to the implication. For $2^{k+1} > (k+1)^3$ to follow from
$2^k > k^3$, the factor of $2$ gained on the left has to outrun the factor
$\left(1 + \frac{1}{k}\right)^3$ gained on the right, and that happens from $k = 4$ onwards.
Below $k = 4$ the step is simply false: at $k = 3$, $2 \cdot 8 = 16$ is not greater than
$4^3 = 64$.

The second threshold belongs to the statement, and it is much later. Exponential growth
eventually beats any power, but "$n^3$" holds out for a surprisingly long time: $2^n$ is behind
$n^3$ at every integer from $2$ to $9$, catches up only at $10$, and the two are within
$2.4$ per cent of each other there. So the base case has to be $10$, not $4$, even though the
step would have worked from $4$.

The general principle is that an induction proves statements from a base case *using* a step,
so the base case must satisfy two independent conditions: the statement has to be true there,
and the step has to be valid from there. The correct starting point is the larger of the two
thresholds, and an item is only interesting when the two thresholds disagree — which is
exactly what happens here.

The isolated value $n = 1$ is the part candidates lose most often, and it is not a trick.
$P(1)$ says $2 > 1$, which is true, and $P(2)$ says $4 > 8$, which is not. An induction
started anywhere cannot reach $n = 1$ going forwards, and there is nothing to induct on going
backwards. The answer set genuinely has two components, and the reason it feels wrong is that
most school induction questions have an answer of the form "all $n \ge N$". Writing the set as
$\{1\} \cup \{n \ge 10\}$ is the only honest description.

Finally, note what the arithmetic in (a) is for. It is not busywork to pad the question: it
establishes both thresholds empirically before the candidate is asked to prove anything about
either, and it is the only place where the failure at $n = 8$ — where the two sides are in the
ratio $1:2$ — becomes visible. A candidate who skips (a) and guesses has no way to know that
$n = 9$ fails.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 4.11 A payout of 2^k occurring with probability 2^-k: the expected value of the uncapped game does not converge, the cap at 2^20 makes it exactly 21, and the probability of recovering the fair entry fee is only one sixteenth, so the expected value and the chance of finishing ahead point in opposite directions
questions.question:
A casino offers the following game. A fair coin is tossed repeatedly until it shows a head for the first time. If that first head appears on toss $k$, the player receives $2^{k}$ dollars. So a head on the first toss pays $2$, a head on the second pays $4$, a head on the third pays $8$, and so on. Let $X$ be the payout, so that $\Pr(X = 2^{k}) = 2^{-k}$ for $k = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ The casino protects itself with a cap: no payout exceeds $2^{20} = 1\,048\,576$ dollars, so a player whose first head arrives on toss $21$ or later receives $2^{20}$ dollars. The entry fee is to be set at the expected payout of the capped game. All answers should be given exactly where the question asks for an exact value, and $2^{20}$ may be left in that form.

(a)

Show that $\Pr(X = 2^{k}) = 2^{-k}$ defines a valid probability distribution on $k = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$, and show that the expected payout of the uncapped game does not converge.

[3]

(b)

Determine the expected payout of the capped game, and hence the fair entry fee, evaluating the contribution of the tail $k \ge 21$ explicitly.

[4]

(c)

Determine the probability that a single play returns at least the fair entry fee, and the probability that a single play returns no more than $\$4$.

[3]

(d)

Explain why a player who decides by maximising expected monetary value and a player who decides by maximising the probability of finishing ahead reach opposite conclusions about paying the fair entry fee. Support your explanation with the expected payout, the probability from part (c), and the standard deviation of the payout.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The probabilities are $2^{-1}, 2^{-2}, 2^{-3}, \ldots$, so their sum is a geometric series with first term $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and ratio $\tfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\sum_{k \ge 1}2^{-k} = \frac{1/2}{1 - 1/2} = 1 \;(M1)(A1).$$Every term is positive and the sum is $1$, so this is a valid distribution.
The expected payout without the cap is
$$\sum_{k \ge 1}2^{k}\cdot 2^{-k} = \sum_{k \ge 1}1 = 1 + 1 + 1 + \cdots \;(M1),$$
and the partial sums are $1, 2, 3, \ldots, n$ after $n$ terms, which grow without bound (A1). The expectation therefore does not converge. The cause is that the payout doubles exactly as fast as the probability halves, so the two factors cancel in every term and nothing is left to make the terms shrink.
(b) With the cap, the payout is $2^{k}$ for $1 \le k \le 20$ and $2^{20}$ for $k \ge 21$. For the first twenty terms the factors again cancel, so each contributes $1$ and the total is $20$ (M1). For the tail,
$$\sum_{k \ge 21}2^{-k} = 2^{-20}, \;(M1)$$
which is the probability that the first head arrives on toss $21$ or later, so the tail contributes
$$2^{20}\cdot 2^{-20} = 1 \;(A1).$$
Hence $\mathbb{E}(X) = 20 + 1 = 21$ dollars, and the fair entry fee is $\$21$ (A1). The cap has turned an infinite expectation into a finite one, and the whole of the tail contributes exactly as much as one of the early terms.
(c) The payout reaches the fee of $\$21$ when $2^{k} \ge 21$, that is when $k \ge 5$, since $2^{4} = 16 < 21$ and $2^{5} = 32 \ge 21$ (M1). Therefore
$$\Pr(X \ge 21) = \sum_{k \ge 5}2^{-k} = 2^{-4} = \frac{1}{16} \;(A1).$$
A play returns no more than $\$4$ when $k \le 2$, so
$$\Pr(X \le 4) = 2^{-1} + 2^{-2} = \frac{3}{4} \;(A1).$$
So the player recovers the fee in one play out of sixteen, and finishes with $\$4$ or less in three plays out of four.
(d) The two players are answering different questions with the same data. The expected-value player asks what the average payout would be over infinitely many plays, and the answer is $\$21$, so at a fee of $\$21$ the game is exactly fair and playing is no worse than not playing (A1). The second player asks what will happen on the single play that is actually available, and from part (c) the probability of finishing ahead is $\tfrac{1}{16}$, while the probability of finishing behind is $\tfrac{15}{16}$ (A1).
The reason the two answers can both be correct is that the mean of a heavily skewed distribution is not a typical value. Computing $\mathbb{E}(X^{2}) = \sum_{k=1}^{20}2^{k} + 2^{20} = (2^{21} - 2) + 2^{20} = 3\,145\,726$ gives
$$\operatorname{Var}(X) = 3\,145\,726 - 21^{2} = 3\,145\,285, \qquad \sigma_{X} \approx 1773.5 \;(A1).$$
A standard deviation of about $1773$ against a mean of $21$ says that a single play is almost always either far below the mean or vastly above it; the mean is produced by the rare large payouts and describes none of the outcomes the player is likely to see. A player who can afford many plays, or who can pool the game with others, is buying the mean and the expected-value argument applies. A player who plays once is buying a $\tfrac{1}{16}$ chance of a good outcome, and the correct decision depends on which of those two situations the player is in (A1).
questions.explanation:
This is the oldest paradox in probability and it is still the sharpest illustration of what an expectation is not. The payout doubles when the probability halves, so the two factors cancel in every single term of the expectation and every term equals one. An infinite series of ones diverges, and the uncapped game has no expected value at all. Nothing is wrong with the calculation; the game genuinely has no fair price in the expected-value sense.

The cap is what makes the question answerable, and it is also what makes it interesting. Twenty terms of the capped expectation each contribute one, giving twenty, and the entire tail beyond the cap contributes one more, because the probability that the first head arrives on or after the twenty-first toss is $2^{-20}$ and the payout in that case is $2^{20}$. That single unit of contribution is easy to lose: a candidate who caps the payout and then sums only the first twenty terms reports a fair price of twenty and is wrong by a dollar, which in this game is a five per cent error on the answer.

The heart of the item is the contrast between the mean and the distribution. At a fee of twenty-one the player is ahead only if the first head takes five or more tosses, and that happens one time in sixteen. Three plays in four return four dollars or less. The standard deviation of the payout, about seventeen hundred and seventy-four dollars against a mean of twenty-one, is the number that makes the point concrete: it is eighty times the mean, which tells the player that the mean is produced by rare enormous outcomes and describes nothing about the play in hand.

The resolution is not that one decision rule is right and the other is wrong. A player who can repeat the game many times, or a syndicate that buys many tickets, is buying the mean, and for them the expected-value argument is the correct one. A player with one play and a limited bank is buying an outcome, and for them the probability of finishing ahead is the relevant quantity. Saying which is which is the judgement the final part is asking for.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: P3 extended problem: series solution of a differential equation with no elementary solution
questions.question:
The function $y$ is defined for all real $x$ by
$$\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = e^{-x^{2}}, \qquad y(0) = 0,$$
and $y$ has a Maclaurin series $y(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n x^{n}$ that converges for all real $x$. Write $t_k = \dfrac{(-1)^{k} x^{2k+1}}{k!\,(2k+1)}$ for $k \ge 0$.

(a)

Show that $a_n = 0$ for every even $n$, and that $a_{2k+1} = \dfrac{(-1)^{k}}{k!\,(2k+1)}$ for every integer $k \ge 0$, so that $y(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} t_k$.

[3]

(b)

Show that $\left|\dfrac{t_{k+1}}{t_k}\right| = \dfrac{x^{2}}{k+1} \cdot \dfrac{2k+1}{2k+3}$, and deduce that $|t_{k+1}| < |t_k|$ for every $k \ge 0$ whenever $|x| \le 0.6$.

[3]

(c)

Hence show that
$$\left|\,y(0.6) - \sum_{k=0}^{3} t_k\,\right| < 5 \times 10^{-5}.$$

[5]

(d)

Hence determine $y(0.6)$ correct to four decimal places, showing that your value is reliable at that accuracy.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Write $y(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} a_n x^{n}$, so $y'(x) = \sum_{n \ge 1} n\,a_n x^{n-1} = \sum_{n \ge 0} (n+1)a_{n+1} x^{n}$ (M1). Also $e^{-x^{2}} = \sum_{k \ge 0} \dfrac{(-1)^{k} x^{2k}}{k!}$, since replacing $x$ by $-x^{2}$ in the exponential series is valid for all real $x$ (A1). Equating coefficients of $x^{n}$ in $\sum_{n \ge 0} (n+1)a_{n+1}x^{n} = \sum_{k \ge 0} \dfrac{(-1)^{k}}{k!} x^{2k}$: the right-hand side has no odd powers, so $(n+1)a_{n+1} = 0$ whenever $n$ is odd, that is $a_n = 0$ for every even $n \ge 2$; and $a_0 = y(0) = 0$ (A1). When $n = 2k$ we get $(2k+1)a_{2k+1} = \dfrac{(-1)^{k}}{k!}$, hence $a_{2k+1} = \dfrac{(-1)^{k}}{k!\,(2k+1)}$ for every $k \ge 0$ (A1). Substituting gives $y(x) = \sum_{k \ge 0} \dfrac{(-1)^{k} x^{2k+1}}{k!\,(2k+1)} = \sum_{k \ge 0} t_k$ (AG).

(b) Using $t_k = \dfrac{(-1)^{k}x^{2k+1}}{k!(2k+1)}$,
$$\frac{t_{k+1}}{t_k} = \frac{(-1)^{k+1}x^{2k+3}}{(k+1)!(2k+3)} \cdot \frac{k!(2k+1)}{(-1)^{k}x^{2k+1}} = -x^{2} \cdot \frac{2k+1}{(k+1)(2k+3)}$$ (M1),
so $\left|\dfrac{t_{k+1}}{t_k}\right| = \dfrac{x^{2}}{k+1} \cdot \dfrac{2k+1}{2k+3}$ (A1). Now $\dfrac{2k+1}{2k+3} < 1$ for every $k \ge 0$, so $\left|\dfrac{t_{k+1}}{t_k}\right| < \dfrac{x^{2}}{k+1} \le \dfrac{x^{2}}{1} = x^{2}$ when $k \ge 0$ and $|x| \le 0.6$; since $0.6^{2} = 0.36 < 1$, we get $|t_{k+1}| < |t_k|$ for every $k \ge 0$ (A1) (AG).

(c) From part (b) the terms $t_k$ alternate in sign, because of the factor $(-1)^{k}$, and their moduli decrease strictly. For such a series the truncation error is bounded by the modulus of the first omitted term (M1). We compute, at $x = 0.6$,
$$t_0 = 0.6, \quad t_1 = -\frac{0.216}{3} = -0.072, \quad t_2 = \frac{0.07776}{10} = 0.007776, \quad t_3 = -\frac{0.0279936}{42} = -0.000666514$$ (M1) (A1),
so $\sum_{k=0}^{3} t_k = 0.5351094857$ (A1). The first omitted term is $t_4 = \dfrac{0.6^{9}}{4! \cdot 9} = \dfrac{0.010077696}{216} = 4.6656 \times 10^{-5}$ (M1), and the alternating-series bound therefore gives
$$\left|\,y(0.6) - \sum_{k=0}^{3} t_k\,\right| \le |t_4| = 4.6656 \times 10^{-5} < 5 \times 10^{-5}$$ (A1) (AG).

(d) Four terms are not enough for four decimal places: the interval they determine is $(0.5351094857 - 0.000046656,\; 0.5351094857 + 0.000046656) = (0.5350628, 0.5351561)$, and this straddles the rounding boundary $0.53515$, so the fourth decimal place is not yet decided (M1). Adding the next term, $t_4 = 0.000046656$, gives $\sum_{k=0}^{4} t_k = 0.5351561417$ with the first omitted term now $|t_5| = \dfrac{0.6^{11}}{5! \cdot 11} = \dfrac{0.0036279706}{1320} = 2.7485 \times 10^{-6}$ (M1), so
$$0.5351533932 < y(0.6) < 0.5351561417,$$
and both endpoints round to $0.5352$; hence $y(0.6) = 0.5352$ to four decimal places (A1) (AG). (The exact value is $\tfrac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\,\mathrm{erf}(0.6) = 0.5351535268$, which lies inside the interval, as it must.)
questions.explanation:
This item is built on a reversal. The equation is separable and the solution is, in principle, available in closed form: $y(x) = \int_0^{x} e^{-t^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}t$. A strong candidate will find that in the first thirty seconds and feel that the problem is over. It is not, because that integral has no elementary antiderivative -- it is the error function -- so the closed form cannot produce the number that part (d) asks for. The method that looks like a concession to approximation is the only one that can answer the question.

The coefficient extraction is routine: substituting a power series into the differential equation and comparing coefficients with the exponential series gives a recurrence in which every even coefficient vanishes, because the right-hand side $e^{-x^{2}}$ has only even powers while the derivative of a power series carries the index shift. The surviving coefficients are $\dfrac{(-1)^{k}}{k!(2k+1)}$, which is the series of the error function in disguise.

What makes the item difficult is the demand for an error bound, and this is where the two halves of the series have to be handled differently. The signs alternate because of the $(-1)^{k}$, and the moduli decrease because the ratio is $\dfrac{x^{2}}{k+1}\cdot\dfrac{2k+1}{2k+3} < \dfrac{x^{2}}{k+1} \le 0.36$ throughout the region of interest. An alternating series with strictly decreasing moduli has its truncation error bounded by the first omitted term -- nothing more and nothing less -- so the whole problem reduces to evaluating one term. That is a strong result and it is why the 'approximate' method wins.

The subtlety that separates a good answer from a correct one is part (d). Four terms give $0.5351095 \pm 0.0000467$, and that interval contains $0.53515$, the boundary between $0.5351$ and $0.5352$. So four terms do not determine the fourth decimal place, even though the error is small. A candidate who quotes $0.5351$ because the first four terms give it will be wrong; a candidate who quotes $0.5352$ from a calculator will be right for the wrong reason. Five terms give $0.5351534 < y(0.6) < 0.5351561$, and now both endpoints round to $0.5352$, which is an answer with a reason attached. The habit being tested is asking how many terms the requested accuracy actually requires, rather than assuming that a small error is a sufficient error.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: P3 extended problem: bounding a series by term-wise telescoping
questions.question:
For an integer $n \ge 1$ write $S_n = \displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{k^{2}}$.

(a)

Show that, for every integer $k \ge 3$,
$$\frac{1}{k^{2}} < \frac{1}{k - \frac{1}{2}} - \frac{1}{k + \frac{1}{2}}.$$

[4]

(b)

Hence show that $S_n < \dfrac{7}{4}$ for every integer $n \ge 1$.

[4]

(c)

Show that the alternative estimate $\dfrac{1}{k^{2}} < \dfrac{1}{k(k-1)}$, valid for $k \ge 2$, gives $S_n < 2 - \dfrac{1}{n}$, and explain why this estimate cannot establish the bound in part (b) for $n \ge 4$.

[3]

(d)

Calculate $S_{20}$ correct to six decimal places, and verify that it is consistent both with the bound proved in part (b) and with the tighter value $\dfrac{33}{20} = 1.65$ that your proof in part (b) actually establishes.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Combining the two fractions on the right-hand side over a common denominator,
$$\frac{1}{k - \frac{1}{2}} - \frac{1}{k + \frac{1}{2}} = \frac{\left(k + \frac12\right) - \left(k - \frac12\right)}{\left(k - \frac12\right)\left(k + \frac12\right)} = \frac{1}{k^{2} - \frac14}$$ (M1) (A1).
Since $k \ge 3$ we have $k^{2} - \tfrac14 < k^{2}$, and both quantities are positive, so taking reciprocals reverses the inequality (M1):
$$\frac{1}{k^{2}} < \frac{1}{k^{2} - \frac14} = \frac{1}{k - \frac{1}{2}} - \frac{1}{k + \frac{1}{2}}$$ (A1).

(b) For $n = 1$ and $n = 2$ we have $S_1 = 1$ and $S_2 = 1 + \tfrac14 = \tfrac54 = 1.25$, both less than $\tfrac74 = 1.75$ (A1).

Now let $n \ge 3$. By part (a),
$$\sum_{k=3}^{n} \frac{1}{k^{2}} < \sum_{k=3}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{k - \frac12} - \frac{1}{k + \frac12}\right)$$ (M1).
The right-hand sum telescopes: writing out the first few terms, $\left(\frac{1}{2.5} - \frac{1}{3.5}\right) + \left(\frac{1}{3.5} - \frac{1}{4.5}\right) + \cdots + \left(\frac{1}{n - 0.5} - \frac{1}{n + 0.5}\right)$, every intermediate term cancels (M1), leaving
$$\sum_{k=3}^{n} \frac{1}{k^{2}} < \frac{1}{\frac52} - \frac{1}{n + \frac12} = \frac{2}{5} - \frac{1}{n + \frac12} < \frac{2}{5} = 0.4$$ (A1).
Therefore
$$S_n = 1 + \frac14 + \sum_{k=3}^{n}\frac{1}{k^{2}} < 1 + \frac14 + \frac25 = \frac{20 + 5 + 8}{20} = \frac{33}{20} = 1.65 < \frac74$$ (A1) (AG).
Since $\tfrac{33}{20} < \tfrac74$, this establishes $S_n < \tfrac74$ for every $n \ge 3$, and the cases $n = 1, 2$ were settled separately, so the bound holds for every integer $n \ge 1$ (AG).

(c) For $k \ge 2$ we have $k(k-1) < k^{2}$, so $\dfrac{1}{k^{2}} < \dfrac{1}{k(k-1)}$ (A1). Also $\dfrac{1}{k(k-1)} = \dfrac{1}{k-1} - \dfrac{1}{k}$, so
$$\sum_{k=2}^{n} \frac{1}{k^{2}} < \sum_{k=2}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{k-1} - \frac{1}{k}\right) = 1 - \frac{1}{n}$$ (M1),
the sum telescoping to $\left(1 - \frac12\right) + \left(\frac12 - \frac13\right) + \cdots + \left(\frac{1}{n-1} - \frac{1}{n}\right)$. Hence $S_n < 1 + 1 - \dfrac{1}{n} = 2 - \dfrac{1}{n}$ (A1).

But $2 - \dfrac{1}{n} \ge \dfrac74$ exactly when $\dfrac{1}{n} \le \dfrac14$, that is when $n \ge 4$. So for $n \ge 4$ this estimate bounds $S_n$ only by a quantity that is at least $\tfrac74$, and therefore cannot show $S_n < \tfrac74$ (AG). The estimate is not wrong -- it is a valid upper bound -- it is simply too weak: every estimate of the form $\dfrac{1}{k^{2}} < \dfrac{1}{(k-a)(k-b)}$ with $ab = 0$ produces a telescoping sum whose total is exactly $2$, and no member of that family can reach $1.75$.

(d) Summing directly,
$$S_{20} = 1 + \frac14 + \frac19 + \cdots + \frac{1}{400} = 1.5961632439\ldots$$ (M1) (A1), so $S_{20} = 1.596163$ to six decimal places (A1). This is consistent with the two bounds: $1.596163 < 1.65 < 1.75$ (AG). Note that the proof of part (b) gives the stronger bound $\tfrac{33}{20}$, and the true limit of the series is $\tfrac{\pi^{2}}{6} = 1.644934\ldots$, which also lies below both bounds, so the numerical value is consistent with the theory as it must be.
questions.explanation:
This problem is about a specific and very common failure of reasoning: having found a bound that is true, concluding that it is the bound you need. The estimate $\dfrac{1}{k^{2}} < \dfrac{1}{k(k-1)}$ is the standard one, it appears in every textbook treatment of the convergence of this series, and it works perfectly for its usual purpose -- showing that the series converges, since it gives $S_n < 2 - 1/n < 2$. What it cannot do is show $S_n < \tfrac74$, because it is an estimate whose total is exactly $2$ and $\tfrac74$ is smaller than $2$. No amount of careful algebra applied to that estimate will produce the target, and this is the sense in which the constraint binds.

The escape is to compare against a slightly wider denominator. Instead of $k(k-1)$ one uses $k^{2} - \tfrac14 = \left(k - \tfrac12\right)\left(k + \tfrac12\right)$, which is larger than $k^{2}$ and still splits into two telescoping pieces. The gain is not large -- the tail from $k = 3$ onwards is bounded by $\tfrac25$ instead of $1$ -- but it is exactly enough, and it is enough because the first two terms are handled exactly rather than estimated. That combination, a sharp estimate where it is available and exact arithmetic where the estimate does not apply, is the transferable technique.

The restriction $k \ge 3$ is not incidental. At $k = 1$ the comparison $1/(k^{2}-\tfrac14) > 1/k^{2}$ would give $\tfrac{1}{0.75} = \tfrac43 > 1$, which is a much weaker statement than the trivial equality $1/1^{2} = 1$; at $k = 2$ it would give $\tfrac{1}{3.75} = 0.2667$ against the exact $0.25$. So the sharpened estimate is worse than useless at the start of the series and essential later, and knowing where to switch from exact values to estimates is the real content of part (b). A candidate who applies the new estimate from $k = 1$ obtains a bound larger than $\tfrac74$ and concludes, wrongly, that the method has failed.

Part (d) is a reality check. The true sum is $\tfrac{\pi^{2}}{6} = 1.6449\ldots$, comfortably below $1.65$, so the bound proved here is not merely valid but reasonably tight -- the gap is about $0.005$. Seeing that the bound is nearly attained is what makes the earlier failure of the $k(k-1)$ estimate understandable rather than mysterious: the true value sits so close to $\tfrac{33}{20}$ that any estimate with slack of order $0.35$ was never going to be good enough.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 5.16 A definite integral whose value is independent of the exponent, by a symmetry substitution
questions.question:
For $n \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}$ define $I_{n} = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{1}{1 + \tan^{n}x}\,dx$.

(a)

By using the substitution $x \mapsto \dfrac{\pi}{2} - x$, show that $I_{1} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

[4]

(b)

Show that $I_{n} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ for every positive integer $n$, so that the value does not depend on the exponent.

[5]

(c)

Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{\sin^{5}x}{\sin^{5}x + \cos^{5}x}\,dx$, justifying the identification you make.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Put $u = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - x$, so $du = -dx$. When $x = 0$, $u = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, and when $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $u = 0$ (M1). Also $\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \cot x = \dfrac{1}{\tan x}$ (M1). Therefore
$$I_{1} = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{1}{1 + \tan x}\,dx = \int_{\pi/2}^{0} \frac{1}{1 + \cot u}\,(-du) = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{1}{1 + \cot u}\,du$$

Simplifying the new integrand (M1):
$$\frac{1}{1 + \cot u} = \frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{\cos u}{\sin u}} = \frac{\sin u}{\sin u + \cos u}$$

Adding the two expressions for $I_{1}$:
$$2I_{1} = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\left(\frac{\cos x}{\sin x + \cos x} + \frac{\sin x}{\sin x + \cos x}\right)dx = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} 1\,dx = \frac{\pi}{2} \tag{AG}$$

so $I_{1} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

(b) The same substitution applies to any $n$ (M1). Writing $c$ for $\cos x$ and $s$ for $\sin x$:
$$I_{n} = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{1}{1 + \tan^{n}x}\,dx = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{\cos^{n}x}{\cos^{n}x + \sin^{n}x}\,dx$$

Under $x \mapsto \dfrac{\pi}{2} - x$ the sine and cosine exchange roles, so (M1)
$$I_{n} = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{\sin^{n}x}{\sin^{n}x + \cos^{n}x}\,dx \tag{M1}$$

Adding the two equal expressions for the same number $I_{n}$:
$$2I_{n} = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\left(\frac{\cos^{n}x}{\cos^{n}x + \sin^{n}x} + \frac{\sin^{n}x}{\sin^{n}x + \cos^{n}x}\right)dx = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} 1\,dx = \frac{\pi}{2} \tag{A1}$$

Both denominators are the same expression, so the two fractions sum to $1$ at every $x$ in the interval. Hence
$$I_{n} = \frac{\pi}{4} \quad\text{for every } n \in \mathbb{Z}^{+} \tag{AG}$$

(c) Divide numerator and denominator by $\cos^{5}x$, which is non-zero on $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ (M1):
$$\frac{\sin^{5}x}{\sin^{5}x + \cos^{5}x} = \frac{\tan^{5}x}{\tan^{5}x + 1} = \frac{1}{1 + \cot^{5}x}$$

That is exactly the integrand of $I_{5}$ after the symmetry substitution, and by part (b) its value is independent of the exponent (M1). So (A1)(A1)
$$\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{\sin^{5}x}{\sin^{5}x + \cos^{5}x}\,dx = \frac{\pi}{4}$$

The identification is legitimate because part (b) established the value for every positive integer exponent, not merely for $n = 5$; the exponent is irrelevant to the result, which is why no antiderivative is ever needed.
questions.explanation:
The item is a proof, and the proof is the point. The integrand has no elementary antiderivative for general $n$, and it gets less tractable as $n$ grows, so a student who begins by looking for one has already taken the wrong route. The way forward is to notice that the interval $[0, \pi/2]$ is symmetric under the reflection that exchanges sine and cosine, and that under that reflection the integrand becomes the complementary fraction with the same denominator.

The single step that makes the argument work is recognising that the reflected integrand shares its denominator with the original. Two fractions with the same denominator and numerators summing to that denominator add to one, so twice the integral is the integral of one, which is $\pi/2$. This is a genuinely different technique from substitution as a way of finding an antiderivative: here the substitution is used to relate the integral to itself, not to simplify the integrand in isolation. A student who has only met substitution as a tool for antidifferentiation may not think of it this way, which is why the item is set as problem-solving rather than as routine integration.

The independence of the exponent is the striking part, and part (b) makes it explicit rather than leaving it as an observation about $n = 1$. Part (c) then tests whether the student can move between the tangent form and the sine-and-cosine form, which is the same identification used in the proof and the practical skill that makes the technique applicable elsewhere. The result generalises further, to any pair of complementary functions, and a student who has followed the argument should be able to see why.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 5.19 A Maclaurin series used as the solution of a differential equation that has none of its own, with the constant term of the right-hand side deciding which coefficient the equation cannot pin down
questions.command_term: Show that, Show that, Determine, Explain
questions.question:
The function $y$ satisfies
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = y^{2} - x, \qquad y(0) = 1.$$
The variables cannot be separated and no elementary function satisfies the equation, so its Maclaurin series
$$y = a_{0} + a_{1}x + a_{2}x^{2} + a_{3}x^{3} + \cdots = \sum_{n \ge 0} a_{n}x^{n}$$
is used instead. Write the coefficient of $x^{n}$ in $y^{2}$ as $c_{n} = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_{k}a_{n-k}$.

(a)

Show that $a_{0} = 1$, that $a_{1} = 1$, and that the equation which determines $a_{2}$ is $2a_{2} = 2a_{1} - 1$, so that $a_{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

[3]

(b)

Show that $a_{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}$ and $a_{4} = \dfrac{7}{12}$, and state the general recurrence that expresses $a_{n+1}$ in terms of $a_{0}, a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n}$.

[4]

(c)

Determine $a_{5}$ and $a_{6}$ as exact fractions, showing the value of the Cauchy coefficient $c_{n}$ you use at each step.

[3]

(d)

If the term $-x$ were deleted the solution would be $y = \dfrac{1}{1 - x}$ and every $a_{n}$ would equal $1$. Explain why $a_{1}$ is still $1$ in this question, and state the smallest value of $n$ for which $a_{n} \ne 1$.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Put $x = 0$ in the differential equation. The left side is $y'(0)$, and the right side is $y(0)^{2} - 0 = 1$, but it is $y(0)$ that the series names directly, so read the initial condition: $a_{0} = y(0) = 1$ (A1).

Now substitute the series into the equation. The left side is
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \sum_{n \ge 0} (n+1)a_{n+1}x^{n},$$
and the right side is $y^{2} - x$, that is $c_{0} + (c_{1} - 1)x + c_{2}x^{2} + c_{3}x^{3} + \cdots$, because $x$ is exactly the term with $n = 1$ and contributes nothing to any other coefficient (M1). Comparing coefficients of $x^{0}$ gives
$$1 \cdot a_{1} = c_{0} = a_{0}^{2} = 1,$$
so $a_{1} = 1$ (A1).

Comparing coefficients of $x^{1}$ gives $2a_{2} = c_{1} - 1$ where $c_{1} = 2a_{0}a_{1} = 2$, so
$$2a_{2} = 2a_{1} - 1 = 2 - 1 = 1, \qquad a_{2} = \frac{1}{2}.$$
The $\mathbf{AG}$ marks the required form of the equation that determines $a_{2}$: $2a_{2} = 2a_{1} - 1$. Deleting the $1$ is the trap the item is built on, and it yields $a_{2} = 1$.

(b) Coefficients of $x^{2}$ and $x^{3}$ (M1):
$$3a_{3} = c_{2} = 2a_{0}a_{2} + a_{1}^{2} = 2(1)\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) + 1 = 2, \qquad a_{3} = \frac{2}{3} \;\; (A1).$$
$$4a_{4} = c_{3} = 2a_{0}a_{3} + 2a_{1}a_{2} = 2(1)\left(\tfrac{2}{3}\right) + 2(1)\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{4}{3} + 1 = \frac{7}{3}, \qquad a_{4} = \frac{7}{12} \;\; (A1).$$

The general recurrence, valid for $n \ge 0$, is
$$(n+1)a_{n+1} = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_{k}a_{n-k} - \delta_{n,1}, \qquad \delta_{n,1} = \begin{cases} 1, & n = 1 \\ 0, & n \ne 1 \end{cases} \;\; (A1).$$
Every coefficient of $y$ appears on the right through the convolution, and the single $1$ subtracts at $n = 1$ and nowhere else.

(c) $n = 4$ gives $5a_{5} = c_{4} = 2a_{0}a_{4} + 2a_{1}a_{3} + a_{2}^{2} = \dfrac{7}{6} + \dfrac{4}{3} + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{14 + 16 + 3}{12} = \dfrac{33}{12} = \dfrac{11}{4}$ (M1), so
$$a_{5} = \frac{11}{20} \;\; (A1).$$
$n = 5$ gives $6a_{6} = c_{5} = 2a_{0}a_{5} + 2a_{1}a_{4} + 2a_{2}a_{3} = \dfrac{11}{10} + \dfrac{7}{6} + \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{33 + 35 + 20}{30} = \dfrac{88}{30} = \dfrac{44}{15}$, so
$$a_{6} = \frac{22}{45} \;\; (A1).$$

The two checks against the derivative route agree with these: differentiating the equation gives $y'' = 2yy' - 1$, so $y''(0) = 2(1)(1) - 1 = 1$ and $a_{2} = \tfrac{y''(0)}{2!} = \tfrac{1}{2}$; and $y''' = 2y'^{2} + 2yy''$, so $y'''(0) = 2 + 2 = 4$ and $a_{3} = \tfrac{4}{3!} = \tfrac{2}{3}$.

(d) The coefficient of $x^{1}$ on the right of the equation is $c_{1} - 1$, and the parameter that this determines is $a_{2}$, not $a_{1}$. The quantity $a_{1}$ is fixed one step earlier, by the constant term: $a_{1} = c_{0} = a_{0}^{2}$, and the deleted term $-x$ contributes nothing at $n = 0$ because its own coefficient sits at $n = 1$ (A1). So $a_{1}$ is decided by the same relation in both problems and stays at $1$ (A1).

The smallest $n$ with $a_{n} \ne 1$ is therefore $n = 2$ (A1), where $a_{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}$ against the value $1$ that $y = 1/(1-x)$ gives. The removal of the $-x$ term shifts every coefficient from $a_{2}$ onwards while leaving $a_{0}$ and $a_{1}$ untouched, which is exactly why a candidate who checks only the first two coefficients against $1/(1-x)$ will believe the two problems agree.
questions.explanation:
The technique here is old and mechanical: put the series in, multiply, compare coefficients. What makes the item hard is a single fact about the shape of the right-hand side, and that fact is easy to see and easy to overlook.

The equation is $y' = y^{2} - x$. The unknown term $y^{2}$ produces a convolution, which is what makes the recurrence long, and the known term $-x$ produces exactly one number in exactly one place. A candidate who has learned "series solution of a differential equation" as a procedure will set up $\sum (n+1)a_{n+1}x^{n} = \sum c_{n}x^{n}$, cancel the two sums, and write $(n+1)a_{n+1} = c_{n}$ for all $n$. That is the whole procedure, it is what the textbook examples do, and it is wrong here. The $-x$ does not disappear; it changes the equation at $n = 1$ alone. The result is $a_{2} = 1$ instead of $\tfrac{1}{2}$, and since every later coefficient is built from the earlier ones, the error propagates: $a_{3}$ comes out as $\tfrac{1}{3}$ rather than $\tfrac{2}{3}$, and the whole series is wrong from the third term on.

Part (d) is what stops the item being a bookkeeping exercise. By asking why $a_{1}$ survives unchanged while $a_{2}$ does not, it forces the candidate to say out loud where in the recurrence the $-x$ acts. The answer is that coefficient comparison at $n = 0$ reads off $a_{1}$ from $a_{0}^{2}$ with no help from the $-x$ at all, so the first two coefficients agree with $1/(1-x)$ and only from $a_{2}$ does the two problems part company. A candidate who tests the first two coefficients will find them right and conclude the rest are right, which is the classic wrong turn, and it is only visible if the question asks for the index.

The numbers are chosen so that the arithmetic of the convolution stays exact in fractions and so that both routes to $a_{2}$ and $a_{3}$ -- the coefficient recurrence and repeated differentiation of the differential equation -- can be run and compared. Running both is the recommended check: they use different machinery and agree, and an agreement between two methods is worth more than re-reading one.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 3.18 Three planes whose behaviour changes at one value of a parameter, at which the system becomes inconsistent rather than underdetermined and the three pairwise intersections become parallel lines
questions.command_term: Show that, Determine, Show that, Determine
questions.question:
Three planes are given by
$$\Pi_{1}: x + y + z = 4, \qquad \Pi_{2}: x + 2y + 3z = 7, \qquad \Pi_{3}: 2x + 3y + kz = 12,$$
where $k$ is a real constant.

(a)

Show that the determinant of the system is $k - 4$, and hence state the single value of $k$ at which the planes fail to meet at a unique point.

[3]

(b)

For $k \ne 4$, determine the unique point of intersection in terms of $k$, and verify your expression by substituting $k = 5$.

[4]

(c)

Show that at $k = 4$ the three planes have no common point, and that each pair meets in a line parallel to the other two.

[3]

(d)

Write down the point common to all three planes for $k \ne 4$ in the limit as $k$ becomes large, and use it to determine the constant on the right-hand side of $\Pi_{3}$ for which the three planes would meet in a line when $k = 4$.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The directions normal to the three planes are $(1,1,1)$, $(1,2,3)$ and $(2,3,k)$. Expanding along the first row (M1):
$$\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & k \end{vmatrix}
= 1(2k - 9) - 1(k - 6) + 1(3 - 4) = 2k - 9 - k + 6 - 1 = k - 4 \;\; (A1).$$
The normals are linearly dependent, and the system fails to have a unique solution, exactly when $k - 4 = 0$, that is at $k = 4$ (A1).

(b) From $\Pi_{1}$ and $\Pi_{2}$, subtracting gives
$$y + 2z = 3, \qquad \text{so} \qquad y = 3 - 2z,$$
and then $x = 4 - y - z = 4 - (3 - 2z) - z = 1 + z$ (M1).

Parameterise with $z = t$: the intersection of $\Pi_{1}$ and $\Pi_{2}$ is the line $(x,y,z) = (1 + t,\; 3 - 2t,\; t)$ (A1). Substituting into $\Pi_{3}$ (M1):
$$2(1 + t) + 3(3 - 2t) + kt = 2 + 2t + 9 - 6t + kt = 11 + (k - 4)t = 12,$$
so
$$t = \frac{1}{k - 4}, \qquad (x, y, z) = \left(1 + \frac{1}{k-4},\; 3 - \frac{2}{k-4},\; \frac{1}{k-4}\right) \;\; (A1).$$

At $k = 5$ this gives $t = 1$ and the point $(2, 1, 1)$. Check: $2 + 1 + 1 = 4$; $2 + 2 + 3 = 7$; $2(2) + 3(1) + 5(1) = 12$. All three equations are satisfied, so the expression is correct.

(c) At $k = 4$, $\Pi_{3}$ becomes $2x + 3y + 4z = 12$. On the line $(1 + t, 3 - 2t, t)$ found in (b),
$$2x + 3y + 4z = 2 + 2t + 9 - 6t + 4t = 11$$
for every $t$ (M1). The constant on the left is $11$ at every point of the line and $12$ is required, so no point of the line lies on $\Pi_{3}$ and the three planes have no common point (A1). Note that $2x + 3y + 4z = 11$ is itself a plane, and it is precisely the plane that contains the whole of $\Pi_{1} \cap \Pi_{2}$.

The pairwise intersections are all parallel to that line. In vector form the direction of $\Pi_{1} \cap \Pi_{2}$ is $(1, -2, 1)$. For $\Pi_{1} \cap \Pi_{3}$: subtracting twice $\Pi_{1}$ from $\Pi_{3}$ gives $y + 2z = 12 - 8 = 4$, so $y = 4 - 2z$ and $x = 4 - y - z = z$, that is $(0, 4, 0) + t(1, -2, 1)$. For $\Pi_{2} \cap \Pi_{3}$: subtracting twice $\Pi_{2}$ from $\Pi_{3}$ gives $-y - 2z = 12 - 14 = -2$, so $y + 2z = 2$, $y = 2 - 2z$ and $x = 7 - 2y - 3z = 3 + z$, that is $(3, 2, 0) + t(1, -2, 1)$ (A1).

Three distinct parallel lines, no two of which meet: the three planes form a triangular prism and the system is inconsistent, not underdetermined.

(d) From (b), as $k$ increases without bound,
$$x \to 1, \qquad y \to 3, \qquad z \to 0, \qquad \text{so the point tends to } (1, 3, 0) \;\; (A1).$$
That is the point of $\Pi_{1} \cap \Pi_{2}$ with $z = 0$, the anchor of the line, and it is the point that every member of the family of intersections as $k$ varies shares (M1).

At $k = 4$ the three planes meet in that line exactly when $\Pi_{3}$ contains it. The line $(1 + t, 3 - 2t, t)$ satisfies $2x + 3y + 4z = 11$ identically, so the required right-hand side is $11$ (A1), that is $\Pi_{3}: 2x + 3y + 4z = 11$. With that constant, $\Pi_{3}$ is the plane spanned by the line and one further direction, the three equations reduce to two independent ones, and the solution set is the line $(1, 3, 0) + t(1, -2, 1)$.

The pattern across the two cases is worth stating: at $k = 4$ the three planes share a line only if the constant is $11$, and if it is anything else they share nothing. The determinant alone told us that something degenerates at $k = 4$; it did not tell us which.
questions.explanation:
The determinant is one number and it answers exactly one question: does the system have a unique solution? It is silent on the other question, which is what happens when it does not, and the gap between those two questions is where this item lives.

The reflexive move, and the one almost every candidate makes, is: the determinant is $k - 4$, so at $k = 4$ the planes must be in a sheaf and the solution set must be a line. That conclusion needs a second fact that has not been checked, namely whether the third plane's constant is compatible with the line the first two already determine. Here the first two planes fix the line $(1 + t, 3 - 2t, t)$, and on that entire line $2x + 3y + 4z = 11$ -- the normal vector $(2, 3, 4)$ is the sum of $(1, 1, 1)$ and $(1, 2, 3)$, so the expression collapses to $4 + 7$ with no $t$ surviving. The constant in the actual third plane is $12$. Eleven is not twelve, and the system is inconsistent: three planes forming a prism, each pair meeting in a line parallel to the other two. Nothing meets anything.

The structure that makes this checkable rather than a matter of luck is that the left-hand side collapses. Whenever the third normal vector is a combination of the first two, the left-hand side of the third equation is fixed on the intersection line, and the whole question reduces to comparing one number with one other number. Part (d) makes that explicit by asking what the constant would have to be, and the answer -- $11$ -- is precisely the value that was computed and discarded in part (c).

The other thing worth noticing is part (b)'s form. The solution is $(1, 3, 0) + \tfrac{1}{k-4}(1, -2, 1)$: the solution point slides along the line direction as $k$ changes, and as $k$ becomes large it stops at the anchor $(1, 3, 0)$. That is the geometric content of the whole question, because $(1, 3, 0)$ is where the degenerate line would have to pass. The algebra of the determinant and the geometry of the prism are two views of one statement, and a candidate who sees the limit will not make the error in part (c).

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 4.4 The effect of one influential point on r and on the regression line, and why a high r does not make a prediction reliable
questions.question:
The table gives the ten pairs of values of $x$ and $y$, and the diagram shows the corresponding scatter diagram with the line of best fit for all ten points. Give all numerical answers correct to three significant figures unless the question says otherwise.

(a)

Describe the relationship between $x$ and $y$ that the diagram suggests, and identify the single point that has the greatest influence on the position of the line of best fit. Justify your choice by reference to the diagram.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the product-moment correlation coefficient $r$ for all ten pairs of values, and find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ in the form $y = mx + c$.

[4]

(c)

The point $(10,\,30)$ is now removed from the data. Find the new value of $r$ and the new regression line, and hence determine the change in the value of $y$ predicted at $x = 12$. Comment on what your answers show about relying on $r$ alone to decide whether a prediction from the line is trustworthy.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) The nine points with the smaller $x$-values lie close to a straight line of positive gradient passing near the origin, so the diagram suggests a strong positive linear relationship (A1). The point $(10,\,30)$ lies well above that line, and it is also the point furthest from the mean of the $x$-values (M1). Because a point at the edge of the range of $x$ exerts the greatest leverage on the line, and because its vertical distance from the line is the largest of the ten, that is the point with the greatest influence on the position of the line of best fit (A1).

(b) For all ten pairs, $n = 10$, $\sum x = 55$, $\sum y = 123$, $\sum x^{2} = 385$ and $\sum xy = 883$, so $S_{xx} = 385 - \tfrac{55^{2}}{10} = 82.5$, $\bar{x} = 5.5$ and $\bar{y} = 12.3$ (M1). Also $S_{xy} = 883 - \tfrac{55 \times 123}{10} = 206.5$, so the gradient is $m = \tfrac{206.5}{82.5} = 2.503$ (A1) and the intercept is $c = 12.3 - 2.503 \times 5.5 = -1.467$ (A1). The regression line is therefore $y = 2.50x - 1.47$. For the correlation coefficient, $S_{yy} = 2095 - \tfrac{123^{2}}{10} = 582.1$, so $r = \tfrac{206.5}{\sqrt{82.5 \times 582.1}} = 0.942$ (A1).

(c) For the nine remaining pairs $n = 9$, $\sum x = 45$, $\sum y = 93$, $\sum x^{2} = 285$ and $\sum xy = 583$, so $S_{xx} = 285 - \tfrac{45^{2}}{9} = 60$, $S_{xy} = 583 - \tfrac{45 \times 93}{9} = 118$ and $S_{yy} = 1195 - \tfrac{93^{2}}{9} = 234$ (M1). The new gradient is $\tfrac{118}{60} = 1.967$, the new intercept is $\tfrac{93}{9} - 1.967 \times 5 = 0.500$, so the new line is $y = 1.97x + 0.500$ (A1), and the new coefficient is $r = \tfrac{118}{\sqrt{60 \times 234}} = 0.996$ (A1). At $x = 12$ the ten-point line predicts $2.503 \times 12 - 1.467 = 28.6$, while the nine-point line predicts $1.967 \times 12 + 0.500 = 24.1$, a change of $4.5$, or about $19\%$ (A1). Removing the point therefore makes $r$ larger while making the gradient $27\%$ steeper in the other direction, so the two summaries move oppositely: $r$ describes how tightly the observed points hug their own line, and says nothing about how far that line will be trusted beyond the measured range, where one point at the edge of the range has already changed the prediction by nearly a fifth (A1).
questions.explanation:
The item is built on a disagreement between two numbers that students are taught to trust together. Removing the tenth point raises $r$ from $0.942$ to $0.996$, which reads as an improvement, and at the same time lowers the gradient from $2.50$ to $1.97$, which changes the prediction at $x = 12$ from $28.6$ to $24.1$. A candidate who reports that 'the correlation improved, so the model is better' has answered a question about fit and been graded on a question about prediction.

The mechanism is leverage. A least-squares line is a weighted compromise, and the weight a point carries in determining the gradient grows with the square of its distance from the mean of $x$. The point at $x = 10$ is the furthest from $\bar{x} = 5.5$ of any point in the set, so it pulls the line towards itself far more strongly than a point of the same vertical distance placed at $x = 5$ would. That is why the influential point here is not simply the point with the largest residual: leverage and residual size are different quantities, and the item rewards a candidate who can separate them.

There is a deliberate trap in the direction of the change. The usual teaching example has an outlier that wrecks a correlation, so the expected move is 'remove it and $r$ goes up, therefore the fit is now sound'. Here $r$ does go up, and the prediction moves further from the trend the other nine points describe, because the removed point was dragging the gradient upwards as well as adding scatter. A candidate who has memorised the direction rather than understood the geometry will write the correct number and the wrong conclusion.

Part (a) is where the diagram earns its place. The table alone cannot show leverage: it takes the picture to see that nine points sit in a band and one sits above the end of it, and to see that the tenth is not merely high but high *and* far to the right. A candidate who works only from the table will often nominate the point with the largest $y$, which here happens to be the same point, and will then be unable to say why.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 2.2 Intersections of the graphs of a decreasing function and its inverse: only one of the three points lies on y = x
questions.question:
A function $f$ is defined on the domain $0 \leq x \leq 6$. Its graph consists of the three straight line segments joining $(0,\,6)$ to $(2,\,3)$, $(2,\,3)$ to $(4,\,2)$ and $(4,\,2)$ to $(6,\,0)$, as shown in the figure.

Because $f$ is decreasing throughout its domain it has an inverse function $f^{-1}$, also defined on $0 \leq x \leq 6$. The graph of $y = f^{-1}(x)$ is the reflection of the graph of $y = f(x)$ in the line $y = x$, and it is drawn dashed in the figure.

(a) Write down the coordinates of two points at which the graphs of $y = f(x)$ and $y = f^{-1}(x)$ intersect, and explain why the two graphs must intersect there.

(b) Find the coordinates of the third point of intersection.

(c) The two graphs enclose two separate regions. Explain why those two regions have equal areas.

(a)

Write down the coordinates of two points of intersection of the graphs of $y = f(x)$ and $y = f^{-1}(x)$, and explain why the graphs must meet there.

[2]

(b)

Find the coordinates of the third point at which the graphs of $y = f(x)$ and $y = f^{-1}(x)$ intersect.

[2]

(c)

Explain why the two regions enclosed between the graphs of $y = f(x)$ and $y = f^{-1}(x)$ have equal areas.

[2]
questions.answer:
(a) The function is decreasing and maps $[0,\,6]$ onto $[0,\,6]$, so it takes its greatest value at the left end of the domain and its least at the right: $f(0) = 6$ and $f(6) = 0$ (M1). Hence $(0,\,6)$ and $(6,\,0)$ both lie on the graph of $y = f(x)$. The graph of $y = f^{-1}(x)$ is the reflection of that graph in $y = x$, and the reflection of $(0,\,6)$ is $(6,\,0)$; so $(6,\,0)$ lies on the graph of the inverse, and it also lies on the graph of $f$. Equivalently $f^{-1}(0) = 6$ and $f^{-1}(6) = 0$. Both points are therefore intersections, and neither lies on $y = x$ (A1).

(b) A fixed point of $f$ is a point of intersection on $y = x$, so solve $f(x) = x$ on each segment. On $0 \leq x \leq 2$, $f(x) = 6 - \tfrac{3}{2}x$, giving $6 - \tfrac{3}{2}x = x$, so $x = 2.4$, which is not in $[0,\,2]$. On $2 \leq x \leq 4$, $f(x) = 4 - \tfrac{1}{2}x$, giving $4 - \tfrac{1}{2}x = x$, so $x = \tfrac{8}{3}$ (M1), which does lie in $[2,\,4]$. On $4 \leq x \leq 6$, $f(x) = 6 - x$, giving $x = 3$, which is not in $[4,\,6]$. The only fixed point is therefore $\left(\tfrac{8}{3},\,\tfrac{8}{3}\right)$ (A1).

(c) Reflection in $y = x$ exchanges the two graphs: it maps the graph of $f$ onto the graph of $f^{-1}$ and the graph of $f^{-1}$ onto the graph of $f$ (M1). The boundary of the first region consists of the arc of $f$ from $(0,\,6)$ to $\left(\tfrac{8}{3},\,\tfrac{8}{3}\right)$ together with the arc of $f^{-1}$ running back; reflecting it gives the arc of $f^{-1}$ from $(6,\,0)$ to $\left(\tfrac{8}{3},\,\tfrac{8}{3}\right)$ together with the arc of $f$ running back, which is exactly the boundary of the second region. A reflection is an isometry and preserves area, so the two regions have equal areas (A1).
questions.explanation:
The item exists because the usual rule of thumb -- a curve meets its reflection on the mirror line -- is a theorem about increasing functions that gets repeated as if it were a fact about all of them. It fails here for a reason that can be stated in one sentence and that a candidate can find without any algebra: a decreasing function that maps $[0,\,6]$ onto $[0,\,6]$ has to send $0$ to $6$ and $6$ to $0$, and those two facts are two points of intersection in their own right. Nothing in the question says the function is decreasing merely to guarantee that an inverse exists; it is decreasing so that the endpoint argument works.

Part (b) then asks for the one point that the usual method does find, and part (c) closes the loop: with three intersections there are two enclosed regions, and a candidate who found only the fixed point has no way to account for the second. The equality of the two areas is not an extra calculation to be performed -- it is the observation that the whole configuration is invariant under the reflection, which sends one region to the other. The figure is load-bearing in a way that figures often are not: it shows the two enclosed regions, and a candidate who has found only one intersection point can see that something is missing before they know what it is.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 5.8 A stationary value that is exactly zero, so a crossing of the axis becomes a touching point and the root count drops by one
questions.question:
The figure shows the graph of $y = f'(x)$ for $0 \leq x \leq 9$. It is made up of the three straight line segments joining $(0,\,0)$ to $(3,\,3)$, $(3,\,3)$ to $(6,\,-3)$ and $(6,\,-3)$ to $(9,\,3)$.

It is given that $f(0) = -2.25$.

(a) Show that $f(7.5) = 0$.

(b) Find the exact value of the other solution of the equation $f(x) = 0$ in the interval $0 \leq x \leq 9$.

(c) State the number of distinct solutions of $f(x) = 0$ in $0 \leq x \leq 9$, and explain why the graph of $y = f(x)$ does not cross the $x$-axis at $x = 7.5$.

(a)

Using the areas between the graph of $y = f'(x)$ and the $x$-axis, show that $f(7.5) = 0$.

[2]

(b)

Find the exact value of the other solution of $f(x) = 0$ in the interval $0 \leq x \leq 9$.

[2]

(c)

State how many distinct solutions $f(x) = 0$ has in $0 \leq x \leq 9$ and explain why the graph of $y = f(x)$ touches rather than crosses the $x$-axis at $x = 7.5$.

[2]
questions.answer:
(a) The area between the graph of $f'$ and the axis from $0$ to $3$ is the triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 3 = 4.5$, and from $3$ to $4.5$, where $f'$ is still positive, it is $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.5 \times 3 = 2.25$. So $f(4.5) = -2.25 + 4.5 + 2.25 = 4.5$ (M1). From $4.5$ to $6$ the signed area is $-\tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.5 \times 3 = -2.25$ and from $6$ to $7.5$ it is another $-2.25$, so $f(7.5) = 4.5 - 2.25 - 2.25 = 0$ (A1).

(b) On $0 \leq x \leq 3$ the graph of $f'$ is the line $f'(x) = x$, so $f(x) = -2.25 + \tfrac{x^{2}}{2}$ on that interval (M1). Setting $f(x) = 0$ gives $x^{2} = 4.5$, so $x = \sqrt{4.5} = \tfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} \approx 2.12$, which lies in $[0,\,3]$. Since $f' \geq 0$ throughout $[0,\,4.5]$ the function is increasing there and this is the only solution in that interval; on $[4.5,\,7.5]$ the function falls from $4.5$ to $0$ without reaching zero again before the endpoint, and on $[7.5,\,9]$ it rises from $0$. The other solution is therefore $x = \tfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$ (A1).

(c) There are two distinct solutions (A1): $x = \tfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$, where the graph crosses the axis, and $x = 7.5$. At $x = 7.5$ the graph of $f'$ crosses the axis, so $f'(7.5) = 0$ and $x = 7.5$ is a stationary point of $f$; part (a) shows that the value there is exactly $0$. The function is decreasing immediately before $7.5$ and increasing immediately after it, so the graph comes down to the axis, touches it at its minimum and turns back up. It does not cross, the root is a repeated one, and the three roots that two turning points suggest never materialise (A1).
questions.explanation:
This is a question about whether zero is a number. The candidate obtains $f(7.5) = 0$ by adding and subtracting areas that are all exact halves, and the temptation at that point is to treat the result as an indication that the arithmetic has gone wrong, because a stationary point that sits exactly on the axis feels like a coincidence. It is not a coincidence: it is the design. The initial value $-2.25$ is chosen to be exactly the negative of the area accumulated by $x = 4.5$ minus the area given back by $x = 7.5$.

Once $f(7.5) = 0$ is established, the root count follows from the sign of $f'$: the function rises through zero once, reaches a maximum, falls to touch the axis at its minimum, and rises again. The answer two is smaller than the three that two turning points suggest, and the missing root is not missing at all -- it has merged with the stationary point. That is the kind of thing a candidate can check: a sketch of $f$ built from the accumulated area makes the touching obvious, and a candidate who sketches it before answering will not need to be told.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 4.13 Bayes' theorem
questions.question:
A component is selected at random from a day's output.

(a)

Find the probability that the component is defective.

[4]

(b)

Given that the component is defective, determine the probability that it was made by machine $M_{2}$.

[4]

(c)

Components are packed in boxes of 20. Find the probability that a box contains at least one defective component.

[4]

(d)

A quality-control inspector tests components one at a time until a defective one is found. Given that the fifth component tested is the first defective one, find the probability that it was made by machine $M_{3}$, and explain why the answer is the same as if the first component tested had been defective.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Let $D$ be the event 'defective'.

$$P(D)=P(M_{1})P(D\mid M_{1})+P(M_{2})P(D\mid M_{2})+P(M_{3})P(D\mid M_{3})$$ (M1)

$$=0.40(0.02)+0.35(0.03)+0.25(0.05)$$ (A1)

$$=0.008+0.0105+0.0125$$ (A1)

$$P(D)=0.031\ \ (3.1\%).$$ (A1)

(b) By Bayes' theorem:

$$P(M_{2}\mid D)=\frac{P(M_{2}\cap D)}{P(D)}=\frac{P(M_{2})P(D\mid M_{2})}{P(D)}$$ (M1)

$$=\frac{0.35(0.03)}{0.031}=\frac{0.0105}{0.031}$$ (A1)

$$=0.3387\ldots$$ (A1)

$$P(M_{2}\mid D)=0.339\ (3\ \text{s.f.})$$ (A1)

(c) Let $X$ be the number of defectives in a box. Then $X\sim\mathrm{B}(20,\,0.031)$. (M1)(A1)

$$P(X\ge1)=1-P(X=0)=1-(1-0.031)^{20}$$ (M1)

$$=1-0.969^{20}=1-0.5326$$ (A1)

$$=0.467\ (3\ \text{s.f.})$$

(d) The fifth component tested is defective, and components 1 to 4 are not. Let $F$ be this event.

$$P(M_{3}\mid F)=\frac{P(M_{3}\cap F)}{P(F)}=\frac{P(M_{3}\cap D)}{P(D)}$$ (M1)(A1)

because $F$ says exactly two things about component 5 — that it is defective, and that components 1–4 are not — and the machine that made component 5 is independent of what was found in components 1–4. So the information about components 1–4 is irrelevant to the question asked, and $F$ reduces to '$D$' for the fifth component.

$$=\frac{0.25(0.05)}{0.031}=\frac{0.0125}{0.031}=0.4032\ldots$$ (A1)

$$P(M_{3}\mid F)=0.403\ (3\ \text{s.f.})$$

Why it is the same as for the first component: whether the defective component turns up first, fifth or fiftieth, the only fact that carries information about its origin is that it *is* defective. The positions of the earlier non-defective components depend on the overall defective rate $P(D)=0.031$, which is the same for every machine's output because the components are mixed before packing; they therefore tell us nothing new about which machine made the one we eventually found. (R1)
questions.explanation:
Parts (a)–(c) are a conventional Bayes-and-binomial exercise. Part (d) is the question.

On seeing 'the fifth component tested is the first defective one', most candidates reach for a geometric distribution and start computing $(0.969)^{4}(0.031)$. That calculation is not wrong, but it is unnecessary: the factor $0.969^{4}$ appears in both the numerator and the denominator and cancels. What survives is exactly the answer to (b)-style question for $M_3$.

The reason is structural, and it is what the question is testing. The components are mixed before packing, so the machine that made any given component is independent of the machine that made any other. Learning that components 1–4 were *not* defective tells you something about the overall defective rate — but that rate is already known ($0.031$) and is the same whichever machine made component 5. So the extra information is genuinely irrelevant to the question asked.

This is the same reason a gambler's 'the roulette wheel hasn't landed on red for ten spins, so red is due' reasoning fails — and it is worth saying out loud in class after marking this.

Classic wrong turns: answering $P(M_3)=0.25$ (ignoring the conditioning entirely); using $P(D\mid M_3)=0.05$ as the answer; and, most commonly, computing the full geometric expression in (d), getting the right number, and then being unable to say *why* the 5 is irrelevant — which forfeits the reasoning mark.

Two further wrong turns belong to part (c). The first is to add the twenty individual defect probabilities and answer $20\times0.031=0.62$; the events overlap, so the complement $1-P(\text{none defective})$ is the correct route. The second is to run the binomial with $p=0.05$, the rate of $M_{3}$, rather than the pooled rate $0.031$; the box is filled from the mixed output of all three machines.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 5.14 Implicit differentiation and related rates
questions.question:
A $13$ m ladder rests against a vertical wall. The foot is pulled horizontally away from the wall at a constant rate of $0.5$ m s$^{-1}$. Let $x$ be the distance of the foot from the wall and $y$ the height of the top above the ground, so that $x^{2}+y^{2}=169$.

(a)

By differentiating $x^{2}+y^{2}=169$ with respect to time $t$, show that $\frac{dy}{dt}=-\frac{x}{y}\frac{dx}{dt}$.

[5]

(b)

Find the rate at which the top of the ladder is descending when the foot is $5$ m from the wall.

[5]

(c)

Find the distance of the foot from the wall when the top of the ladder is descending at exactly $1$ m s$^{-1}$.

[6]
questions.answer:
Differentiate $x^{2}+y^{2}=169$ implicitly with respect to $t$: $2x\frac{dx}{dt}+2y\frac{dy}{dt}=0$, so $\frac{dy}{dt}=-\frac{x}{y}\frac{dx}{dt}$ (M1)(A1)(A1)(AG). This is the related-rates equation that links the two speeds through the geometry of the ladder.

When $x=5$ we have $y=\sqrt{169-25}=\sqrt{144}=12$ (M1). With $\frac{dx}{dt}=0.5$, $\frac{dy}{dt}=-\frac{5}{12}(0.5)=-\frac{5}{24}$ m s$^{-1}$ (A1)(AG), so the top of the ladder descends at $\frac{5}{24}$ m s$^{-1}$, approximately $0.208$ m s$^{-1}$.

Set $\frac{dy}{dt}=-1$. Then $-\frac{x}{y}(0.5)=-1$, giving $\frac{x}{y}=2$ and hence $x=2y$ (M1)(A1). Substitute into the constraint: $(2y)^{2}+y^{2}=5y^{2}=169$, so $y^{2}=\frac{169}{5}$ and $y=\sqrt{\frac{169}{5}}$. Therefore $x=2\sqrt{\frac{169}{5}}\approx 11.63$ m (M1)(A1)(AG). As a check, with $x=2\sqrt{169/5}$ we have $x^{2}+y^{2}=4\cdot\frac{169}{5}+\frac{169}{5}=\frac{5\cdot 169}{5}=169$, confirming the constraint. The foot lies between $0$ and $13$, so the configuration is physically valid. The sign convention is that a negative rate of change denotes descent of the top, which is why the requested answer is reported as a positive speed of descent. The sign convention is that a negative rate of change denotes descent of the top, which is why the requested answer is reported as a positive speed of descent.
questions.explanation: The ladder, wall and ground form a right triangle whose hypotenuse is fixed at $13$, so $x$ and $y$ are not independent: $x^{2}+y^{2}=169$. The chain rule applied to time turns this algebraic constraint into a differential one linking the two rates, which is the essence of related-rates problems. Part (b) is the standard forward direction: given the position, find the rate. Part (c) reverses it, asking for the position that produces a given rate, which most candidates only practise forwards and so often mishandle the algebra that leads to $x=2y$. The negative sign throughout means the top moves down exactly as the foot moves out, and the magnitude of the rate blows up as $x\to 13$ (where $y\to 0$), a nice reminder that the formula breaks exactly when the ladder is flat against the wall. The implicit-differentiation step is the lever: without differentiating the constraint with respect to time there is no way to connect the two speeds, and substituting the known rate too early loses the general relationship needed for part (c). Keeping the symbolic relation until the end is what makes part (c) tractable rather than a guessing game, and it is the habit the question is meant to build. Keeping the symbolic relation until the end is what makes part (c) tractable rather than a guessing game, and it is the habit the question is meant to build.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 5.15 Derivatives and integrals of inverse trigonometric functions
questions.question:
Let $y=\arctan x$.

(a)

By writing $x=\tan y$ and differentiating implicitly with respect to $x$, show that $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}$.

[5]

(b)

Hence find the indefinite integral of $\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}$ with respect to $x$.

[5]

(c)

Evaluate the definite integrals $\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}\,dx$ and $\int_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}\,dx$, giving exact answers.

[6]
questions.answer:
Write $x=\tan y$, so $\frac{dx}{dy}=\sec^{2}y$ (M1). By the chain rule $1=\sec^{2}y\,\frac{dy}{dx}$, giving $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\sec^{2}y}$ (A1). Using the identity $\sec^{2}y=1+\tan^{2}y=1+x^{2}$ we obtain $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}$ (A1)(AG). This is the derivative of $\arctan x$, derived rather than recalled.

Because integration reverses differentiation, $\int\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}\,dx=\arctan x+C$ (M1)(A1)(AG), where the constant of integration is essential and must be stated.

Thus $\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}\,dx=\arctan 1-\arctan 0=\frac{\pi}{4}-0=\frac{\pi}{4}$ (M1)(A1), and $\int_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}\,dx=\arctan(\sqrt{3})-\arctan 1=\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{12}$ (A1)(AG). Exact multiples of $\pi$ are required; decimal approximations alone are not sufficient for full credit, though a numerical check such as $0.7854$ and $0.2618$ may be offered as confirmation. The indefinite integral also follows by the substitution $x=\tan u$, $dx=\sec^{2}u\,du$, which reduces the integrand to $1$ and gives $\arctan x+C$, confirming the result by a second method. For the definite integrals the antiderivative is continuous on the closed interval, so the fundamental theorem applies directly with no improper-integral care required. The continuity of the antiderivative on the whole interval guarantees that the endpoint evaluation is valid and that no singularity occurs within the range of integration, so both definite integrals are proper. The method also shows why the antiderivative is unique up to the additive constant, since any two antiderivatives of the same function differ by a constant.
questions.explanation: The derivative of $\arctan x$ is not handed to the candidate on the SL formula sheet, so it must be reconstructed. The trick is to invert the definition: set $x=\tan y$ and differentiate implicitly with respect to $x$, which turns a transcendental derivative into the algebraic identity $\sec^{2}y=1+\tan^{2}y$. Once the derivative is known, the indefinite integral in part (b) is immediate, and the two definite integrals in part (c) are just the standard arctangent values at $1$ and $\sqrt{3}$. The classic errors are to 'remember' the derivative as $1/\sqrt{1+x^{2}}$ (confusing it with the derivative of arcsine) or to drop the $+C$ in part (b), and to give decimal approximations instead of the exact multiples $\pi/4$ and $\pi/12$ in part (c). The derivation is the lever: the item is unsolvable by recall alone but becomes routine once the implicit step is seen, and it reinforces the inverse relationship between differentiation and integration that underpins the whole of Topic 5. A useful consolidation is that every inverse-trigonometric derivative can be obtained this way, so the method generalises far beyond arctangent. Practising the derivation builds the habit of reconstructing formulas under exam pressure, when the formula booklet may not list the exact case required. Reassuringly, both the implicit-differentiation route and the tangent-substitution route arrive at the same antiderivative, which is a useful cross-check, and this convergence deepens the student's confidence in the result.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 1.14 Complex conjugate roots of polynomial equations
questions.question:
Let $P(z)=z^{3}+pz^{2}+qz+r$, where $p$, $q$ and $r$ are real numbers.

(a)

Explain why, if $z_{0}$ is a non-real root of $P$, then $\bar z_{0}$ is also a root of $P$, and deduce that $P$ has exactly one real root.

[3]

(b)

Suppose $P$ has a root of the form $z_{0}=ti$, where $t$ is a non-zero real number. Show that $r=pq$ and that $q>0$.

[4]

(c)

Hence determine the value of $k$ for which $z^{3}-3z^{2}+kz-12$ has a root of the form $ti$ with $t\neq0$, and find all three roots in that case.

[4]

(d)

Determine all real values of $m$ for which $z^{3}+mz^{2}+mz+1$ has a non-real purely imaginary root, and find all the roots of the cubic in each such case.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) Since $p$, $q$ and $r$ are real, conjugating the equation $P(z_{0})=0$ gives $\overline{P(z_{0})}=0$. Conjugation respects sums and products with real coefficients, so $\overline{P(z_{0})}=P(\bar z_{0})$. (M1) Hence $P(\bar z_{0})=0$, so $\bar z_{0}$ is also a root. (A1)

If $z_{0}$ is non-real then $z_{0}\neq\bar z_{0}$, so $P$ has at least the two distinct non-real roots $z_{0}$ and $\bar z_{0}$. A cubic has exactly three roots counted with multiplicity; if the third root were also non-real, its conjugate would be a fourth root. Hence the third root is real, so $P$ has exactly one real root. (R1)(A1)

(b) Let $z_{0}=ti$ with $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and $t\neq0$. Substituting,

$$P(ti)=(ti)^{3}+p(ti)^{2}+q(ti)+r=-t^{3}i-pt^{2}+qti+r.$$ (M1)

So $P(ti)=\left(r-pt^{2}\right)+\left(qt-t^{3}\right)i=0$, and both the real and imaginary parts must vanish. (A1)

The imaginary part gives $t(q-t^{2})=0$; since $t\neq0$ this forces $t^{2}=q$, and therefore $q=t^{2}>0$. (A1) The real part gives $r-pt^{2}=0$, so $r=pt^{2}=pq$. (A1) *(AG)*

(c) Here $p=-3$, $q=k$ and $r=-12$. The condition $r=pq$ becomes $-12=-3k$, so $k=4$, and $q=k=4>0$ is satisfied. (M1)(A1) Then $t^{2}=q=4$, so the purely imaginary roots are $\pm2i$. The third root is real and equals $-p=3$, since the sum of the roots of $z^{3}+pz^{2}+qz+r$ is $-p$. (M1) Indeed $(z-3)(z^{2}+4)=z^{3}-3z^{2}+4z-12$, so the roots are $3$, $2i$ and $-2i$. (A1)

(d) For $z^{3}+mz^{2}+mz+1$ we have $p=m$, $q=m$ and $r=1$. The necessary condition $r=pq$ gives $1=m^{2}$, so $m=\pm1$. (M1)(A1) But the condition from (b) also requires $q>0$, that is $m>0$, so $m=-1$ must be rejected. (M1)

Indeed for $m=-1$ the cubic is $z^{3}-z^{2}-z+1=(z-1)^{2}(z+1)$, whose roots $1$, $1$ and $-1$ are all real, so it has no purely imaginary root. (A1) Hence the only admissible value is $m=1$, and then $z^{3}+z^{2}+z+1=(z+1)(z^{2}+1)$, with roots $-1$, $i$ and $-i$. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The conjugate-root theorem is usually met as a fact to quote. Here it is used three times in different ways, and the last use separates candidates who understand it from those who have memorised it.

Part (a) is the theorem itself, with a small but real subtlety: the deduction that there is exactly one real root uses the fact that a cubic has three roots counted with multiplicity, so a non-real root consumes its conjugate as a second root and leaves precisely one. Students who argue from the graph, or who say 'the other roots are complex' without counting, miss the point.

Part (b) is the technical heart. Substituting $z=ti$ splits the cubic into a real part and an imaginary part, and the imaginary part factors as $t(q-t^{2})$. Because the root is assumed non-zero, $t\neq0$, and this forces $q=t^{2}>0$. The real part then forces $r=pt^{2}=pq$. So the single algebraic condition $r=pq$, together with the inequality $q>0$, is necessary for a purely imaginary root.

Part (c) applies the condition to a concrete cubic and produces the clean factorisation $(z-3)(z^{2}+4)$.

Part (d) is the lever. The condition $r=pq$ alone admits two values, $m=\pm1$, because $r=pq$ becomes $1=m^{2}$. The inequality $q>0$ is not decoration: it is what removes $m=-1$. And the reason is visible when the rejected case is factored, since $z^{3}-z^{2}-z+1$ has roots $1,1,-1$, all real, so it has no purely imaginary root at all. A candidate who treats $r=pq$ as sufficient will confidently answer $m=\pm1$ and be wrong.

The classic wrong turns are: forgetting that a non-real root is a pair; dividing by $t$ without recording that $t\neq0$; using only $r=pq$ and ignoring $q>0$ in (d); and mis-signing Vieta, since the sum of the roots of $z^{3}+pz^{2}+qz+r$ is $-p$, not $p$. A useful check is that $(z+p)(z^{2}+q)=z^{3}+pz^{2}+qz+pq$ reproduces the cubic exactly, which is why the condition is both necessary and sufficient.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 2.6 The quadratic function
questions.question:
For each real number $m$, define $f(x)=(m-1)x^{2}+2(m+1)x+(m+2)$. The family of curves $y=f(x)$ changes character as $m$ varies, and several parts of this question ask you to describe that change.

(a)

Show that when $m=1$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is a straight line, and state its equation.

[3]

(b)

For $m\neq1$, find the coordinates of the vertex of $y=f(x)$, giving your answer in terms of $m$.

[5]

(c)

Determine the set of values of $m$ for which the graph of $y=f(x)$ does not meet the $x$-axis.

[5]

(d)

Explain why, for every $m>1$, the vertex lies below the $x$-axis, and deduce the number of real roots of $f(x)=0$.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Setting $m=1$ makes the coefficient of $x^{2}$ equal to zero, so the quadratic degenerates to a linear expression (M1). Substituting gives $f(x)=2(1+1)x+(1+2)=4x+3$ (A1). Hence the graph is the straight line $y=4x+3$ (A1) *(AG)*. The coefficient of $x^{2}$ is the only term that can vanish, so this is the single value at which the family changes type.

(b) Completing the square for $m\neq1$, write $f(x)=(m-1)\left[x^{2}+\frac{2(m+1)}{m-1}x\right]+(m+2)$ (M1). The bracket becomes $\left(x+\frac{m+1}{m-1}\right)^{2}-\left(\frac{m+1}{m-1}\right)^{2}$ (A1), so the axis of symmetry is $x=-\frac{m+1}{m-1}$ (A1). Substituting this value and simplifying gives $-\frac{m+3}{m-1}$ (M1)(A1). The vertex is therefore $\left(-\frac{m+1}{m-1},-\frac{m+3}{m-1}\right)$. This is the standard vertex formula for a parabola, and it is valid for every value of $m$ except the one excluded by the question.

(c) The discriminant is $[2(m+1)]^{2}-4(m-1)(m+2)$ (M1) $=4(m+1)^{2}-4(m-1)(m+2)$ (A1) $=4(m+3)$ (A1). The graph misses the $x$-axis exactly when the discriminant is negative, so $4(m+3)<0$ (M1), giving $m<-3$ (A1). Because the discriminant is linear in $m$, its sign changes at exactly one value, so the set of such $m$ is a single ray rather than a bounded interval.

(d) For $m>1$ the leading coefficient $m-1$ is positive, so the parabola opens upwards (A1). The $y$-coordinate of the vertex is $-\frac{m+3}{m-1}$, and both $m+3$ and $m-1$ are positive, so this value is negative (R1). An upward parabola whose vertex lies below the $x$-axis must cross the axis twice (M1), so $f(x)=0$ has two distinct real roots (A1), consistent with $4(m+3)>0$. The sign of the discriminant gives independent confirmation of this count, so the number of real roots is exactly two.
questions.explanation:
The trap is that the leading coefficient depends on the parameter. Most candidates treat $f$ as a quadratic throughout, and part (a) is designed to catch exactly that: when $m=1$ there is no $x^{2}$ term at all, and the curve is a line. A candidate who divides by $m-1$ without first checking that $m\neq1$ will produce an undefined vertex.

The second trap is the discriminant. Expanding $[2(m+1)]^{2}-4(m-1)(m+2)$ is routine, but the cancellation is delicate: the $m^{2}$ terms disappear and leave the linear expression $4(m+3)$. Candidates who lose a factor of four, or who expand $(m-1)(m+2)$ carelessly, will get the wrong threshold. The correct reading is that the sign of the discriminant is controlled entirely by $m+3$, so the boundary is at $m=-3$, not at $m=1$ or $m=0$.

Part (d) is a reasoning question that rewards understanding the shape of a parabola. The vertex formula from part (b) is reused, but the point is not to compute anything new: it is to notice that an upward-opening parabola whose lowest point is below the axis has to cross the axis on both sides. The discriminant from part (c) confirms this, since $m>1$ makes $4(m+3)$ positive.

Classic wrong turns include assuming the family is always a parabola; writing the vertex with the wrong signs; treating 'does not meet the $x$-axis' as 'discriminant less than or equal to zero'; and in part (d) concluding that there are no real roots because the vertex is negative. A candidate who sketches the family for two or three values of $m$ will see the transition from a line at $m=1$ to very narrow parabolas for values of $m$ close to one. The family is a useful illustration of how a single parameter can change the nature of a curve.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 2.9 Exponential functions and their graphs and 2.10 Solving equations analytically
questions.question:
Let $f(x)=3^{x}$ and $g(x)=3^{-x}$.

(a)

Sketch the graphs of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ on the same axes, stating the equation of the asymptote and the coordinates of the $y$-intercept of each.

[4]

(b)

Show that the graph of $y=g(x)$ is the reflection of the graph of $y=f(x)$ in the $y$-axis, and find the coordinates of their point of intersection.

[4]

(c)

Find the two transformations that map the graph of $y=f(x)$ onto the graph of $y=3^{x-2}+1$, and state the equation of the asymptote and the coordinates of the $y$-intercept of the image.

[4]

(d)

Determine the set of values of $k$ for which $3^{2x}-4\cdot3^{x}+k=0$ has two distinct real solutions.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Both curves have the negative $x$-axis as a horizontal asymptote, that is $y=0$ (A1). Since $3^{0}=1$, both pass through $(0,1)$ (A1). The graph of $f$ rises from left to right without bound, while the graph of $g$ falls from left to right, tending to zero (A1)(A1). Both curves lie entirely above the $x$-axis, so neither ever meets it, and the only point they share is the intercept.

(b) Replacing $x$ by $-x$ in $f$ gives $f(-x)=3^{-x}=g(x)$ (M1)(A1), so $g$ is the reflection of $f$ in the $y$-axis. At an intersection $3^{x}=3^{-x}$ (M1), so $3^{2x}=1$ and hence $x=0$ (A1); the point is $(0,1)$. The reflection is a symmetry of this particular pair of curves, and it does not depend on the value of the base.

(c) We have $3^{x-2}+1=f(x-2)+1$. The graph of $f(x-2)$ is obtained by translating $y=f(x)$ by $2$ units in the positive $x$-direction (A1), and adding $1$ translates the result by $1$ unit in the positive $y$-direction (A1). The asymptote $y=0$ moves to $y=1$ (A1), and the $y$-intercept is $3^{0-2}+1=\frac{1}{9}+1=\frac{10}{9}$, that is $\left(0,\frac{10}{9}\right)$ (A1). Because both operations are translations, their order is immaterial, and the image is the same curve either way.

(d) Put $u=3^{x}$, so $u>0$ and the equation becomes $u^{2}-4u+k=0$ (M1). Two distinct real solutions in $x$ require two distinct positive roots $u$ (R1). The discriminant $16-4k$ must be positive, giving $k<4$ (M1)(A1), and the product of the roots, equal to $k$, must be positive, giving $k>0$ (A1). Hence $0<k<4$ (A1). The product condition is the one that is easily overlooked, and it is what removes the negative values of $k$ from the answer.
questions.explanation:
The question concerns two exponential curves that are mirror images of each other, but the difficulty is concentrated in the final part, where a hidden quadratic in $3^{x}$ appears. Parts (a) to (c) are standard graph work and are there to establish the vocabulary of asymptote, intercept and transformation before the algebraic twist.

The most common error is in part (d). Candidates set the discriminant of $u^{2}-4u+k=0$ to be positive, obtain $k<4$, and stop. That is necessary but not sufficient: the substitution $u=3^{x}$ restricts $u$ to positive values, so both roots of the quadratic must be positive. For a quadratic with leading coefficient one, the product of the roots equals $k$, so positivity of the product gives $k>0$. The sum of the roots is $4$, which is positive automatically, so no further condition is needed. The answer is therefore the open interval $0<k<4$.

A candidate who reasons only about the discriminant will include negative values of $k$ in the answer. At $k=-1$, for instance, the quadratic $u^{2}-4u-1=0$ has one positive and one negative root, and only the positive root corresponds to a real $x$, so there is exactly one solution rather than two. This is the fastest numerical check.

Other traps include treating the asymptote of $3^{x-2}+1$ as $y=0$; computing the $y$-intercept as $3^{-2}$ and forgetting the $+1$; and in part (b) assuming the curves meet where the graph crosses the axis. The base three is a red herring, since every positive base other than one behaves in the same way and the structure of the answer does not depend on it. The base is arbitrary, so the result is really a statement about all exponential functions whose base is greater than one.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
