The difficulty is almost entirely in the set-up, not the calculus. Two things have to be noticed before any standard technique applies:

1. The constant-area condition is a statement about the *tangent*, so the first job is to convert a geometric sentence into an equation involving $y'$. Students often try to use the length $\mathrm{AP}$ instead of the perpendicular height $y$, which produces an unworkable expression.
2. The resulting differential equation, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\dfrac{y^{2}}{xy-4}$, is not separable and is not linear in $y$. It *is* linear in $x$. Recognising that $\dfrac1y\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}y}-\dfrac{x}{y}\right)$ is exactly the derivative of $\dfrac{x}{y}$ is the single step that unlocks the question — this is the same observation that stands behind the integrating-factor formula, but here it has to be made explicitly rather than recalled.

The data were chosen so that the given point $(1,\,4)$ is the leftmost point of the curve, which is why part (d) collapses to the neat value $x=1$; a candidate who sketches the curve will see that the curve is a hyperbola with two branches meeting at $(1,\,4)$.

Classic wrong turns: assuming $\mathrm{A}$ lies between $\mathrm{O}$ and the foot of the perpendicular from $\mathrm{P}$; treating $k$ as zero; and, in (d), differentiating $x=\tfrac2y+\tfrac y8$ with respect to $x$ rather than $y$.

Two further wrong turns are common in (d). The first is to mis-pair the AM–GM terms and set $\frac2y=8y$ instead of $\frac2y=\frac y8$, giving the spurious minimum $y=\tfrac12$; the correct pairing gives $y^{2}=16$. The second is to accept the stationary point without checking the domain: the curve lies in the first quadrant, so only $y>0$ is admissible.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: P3 extended problem: constrained optimisation with a cost parameter
questions.question:
A closed cylindrical can is to be manufactured with a fixed volume $V$. The curved surface is made from a material costing $p$ per unit area. The two circular ends are made from a thicker material costing $kp$ per unit area, where $k > 0$ is a constant. Let the can have base radius $r$ and height $h$.

(a)

Show that the total material cost can be written as
$$C(r) = 2\pi p k r^{2} + \frac{2pV}{r}, \qquad r > 0.$$

[4]

(b)

Determine the value of $r$ that minimises $C$, and show that it is indeed a minimum. Give your answer in terms of $V$, $k$ and $\pi$.

[5]

(c)

Hence show that the ratio of the height to the radius at the optimum is $2k$, independent of $V$ and $p$. Comment on what this predicts when $k=1$ and when $k$ is very large, and explain why both predictions are physically sensible.

[6]
questions.answer:
(a) The two circular ends have total area $2\pi r^{2}$ and cost $kp$ per unit area, contributing $2\pi r^{2}\cdot kp$. (A1) The curved surface has area $2\pi r h$, contributing $2\pi r h\cdot p$. (A1) The volume is fixed: $\pi r^{2}h = V$, so $h = \dfrac{V}{\pi r^{2}}$. (M1)
$$C = 2\pi p k r^{2} + 2\pi r p\cdot\frac{V}{\pi r^{2}} = 2\pi p k r^{2} + \frac{2pV}{r}$$ (A1)(AG)

(b) Differentiating with respect to $r$: (M1)
$$C'(r) = 4\pi p k r - \frac{2pV}{r^{2}}$$
Setting $C'(r) = 0$: (M1)
$$4\pi p k r = \frac{2pV}{r^{2}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad r^{3} = \frac{2pV}{4\pi p k} = \frac{V}{2\pi k}$$
$$r = \left(\frac{V}{2\pi k}\right)^{1/3}$$ (A1)
To confirm it is a minimum: (M1)
$$C''(r) = 4\pi p k + \frac{4pV}{r^{3}} > 0 \quad \text{for all } r>0$$
since $p$, $k$ and $V$ are all positive, so the stationary point is a minimum. (A1) (It is the only stationary point on $r>0$, and $C\to\infty$ both as $r\to0^{+}$ and as $r\to\infty$, so it is the global minimum.)

(c) Using $h = \dfrac{V}{\pi r^{2}}$ and $r^{3} = \dfrac{V}{2\pi k}$: (M1)
$$\frac{h}{r} = \frac{V}{\pi r^{3}} = \frac{V}{\pi\cdot\dfrac{V}{2\pi k}} = \frac{V\cdot 2\pi k}{\pi V} = 2k$$ (M1)(A1)(AG)
The ratio depends on $k$ only: $V$ and $p$ both cancel. (A1)

When $k=1$ the ends and the curved surface cost the same per unit area, and the optimum has $h = 2r$, so the height equals the diameter: the can is as tall as it is wide. (A1) This is the familiar equal-cost result and is sensible because the shape is then equally 'spread' in every direction.

When $k$ is very large the ends are very expensive relative to the curved surface, so the optimum makes the ends small and the can tall and thin, consistent with $h/r = 2k$ growing without bound. (A1) Conversely, if the ends were very cheap, $k\to0$ and the can becomes short and wide, which also matches intuition. The limiting cases therefore both confirm the result.
questions.explanation:
The interesting result here is not the optimal radius but the optimal *shape*, and the question is arranged so that the shape is what survives. Once the volume constraint is used to eliminate the height, the cost is a function of one variable and differentiating it is routine. What is not routine is noticing that the answer should be expressed as a ratio: dividing $h$ by $r$ makes both $V$ and $p$ cancel, leaving $h/r = 2k$. That is a genuinely useful engineering statement, because it says the proportions of the cheapest can depend only on how much more the end material costs than the side material, and not at all on how big the can is or on the absolute price of the material.

This is why a student who reaches for a calculator early is punished. If $V$ and $p$ are given numerical values, the arithmetic goes through and produces a correct radius and height, but the cancellation is invisible and the general result is lost. The question deliberately withholds numerical values for $V$ and $p$ and supplies only the dimensionless parameter $k$, which is a strong hint about what the answer should look like. Getting a dimensionless quantity on one side of an equation and only dimensionless quantities on the other is a reliable way to check that an optimisation has been set up correctly.

The two limiting cases are not decorative. At $k=1$ the answer $h=2r$ reproduces the well-known result that the cheapest equal-cost can has its height equal to its diameter, which gives a student something to recognise. As $k$ grows the can becomes tall and thin, which is what a manufacturer would do if the end material were very expensive; as $k$ shrinks it becomes short and wide. That both limits behave sensibly is a check on the algebra that costs nothing and catches sign errors.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 1.13 Complex numbers in polar and Euler form
questions.question:
Let $\alpha=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{5}}$, so that $\alpha$ is a non-real fifth root of unity.

(a)

Show that $1+\alpha+\alpha^{2}+\alpha^{3}+\alpha^{4}=0$.

[3]

(b)

Show that $\alpha^{k}+\alpha^{-k}=2\cos\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi k}{5}\right)$ for $k=1$ and $k=2$.

[3]

(c)

Hence show that $\cos\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\right)+\cos\!\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\right)=-\dfrac12$.

[3]

(d)

Hence show that $\cos\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\right)=\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}{4}$.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) $\alpha^{5}=\left(e^{2\pi i/5}\right)^{5}=e^{2\pi i}=1$ and $\alpha\neq1$. (A1)

The terms form a geometric series with first term $1$ and ratio $\alpha$, so

$$1+\alpha+\alpha^{2}+\alpha^{3}+\alpha^{4}=\frac{\alpha^{5}-1}{\alpha-1}$$ (M1)

$$=\frac{1-1}{\alpha-1}=0\quad(\alpha\neq1).\ \ \textbf{(A1)}$$ *(AG)*

(b) By Euler's form, $\alpha^{k}=e^{2\pi ik/5}=\cos\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi k}{5}\right)+i\sin\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi k}{5}\right)$ (M1)

and $\alpha^{-k}=e^{-2\pi ik/5}=\cos\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi k}{5}\right)-i\sin\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi k}{5}\right)$, since cosine is even and sine is odd. (A1)

Adding, the imaginary parts cancel:

$$\alpha^{k}+\alpha^{-k}=2\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi k}{5}\right).\ \ \textbf{(A1)}$$ *(AG)*

(c) Since $\alpha^{5}=1$ we have $\alpha^{4}=\alpha^{-1}$ and $\alpha^{3}=\alpha^{-2}$. (M1)

Grouping the result of (a) as $1+(\alpha+\alpha^{4})+(\alpha^{2}+\alpha^{3})=0$ and applying (b) with $k=1$ and $k=2$:

$$1+2\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}\right)+2\cos\!\left(\frac{4\pi}{5}\right)=0$$ (A1)

$$\Rightarrow\ \cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}\right)+\cos\!\left(\frac{4\pi}{5}\right)=-\frac12.\ \ \textbf{(A1)}$$ *(AG)*

(d) Using the double-angle identity $\cos2\theta=2\cos^{2}\theta-1$ with $\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$:

$$\cos\!\left(\frac{4\pi}{5}\right)=2\cos^{2}\!\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}\right)-1.$$ (M1)

Let $c=\cos\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\right)$. Substituting into (c):

$$c+2c^{2}-1=-\frac12\ \Rightarrow\ 2c^{2}+c-\frac12=0\ \Rightarrow\ 4c^{2}+2c-1=0$$ (M1)(A1)

$$c=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{4+16}}{8}=\frac{-2\pm2\sqrt5}{8}=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt5}{4}$$ (A1)

Since $0<\dfrac{2\pi}{5}<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, we have $c>0$, so

$$\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}\right)=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4}.\ \ \textbf{(A1)}$$ *(AG)*
questions.explanation:
Nothing here is individually difficult; the question is hard because of the length of the chain and because each part depends on the one before. There is no calculator, so a candidate who cannot see where the chain is going has no way to check whether an intermediate result is right.

The two places where candidates come off the rails:

1. Part (c) is where the 'hence' is real. Recognising that $\alpha^{4}=\alpha^{-1}$ (and not, say, $\overline{\alpha}$ used vaguely) is what turns a statement about complex numbers into a statement about cosines. Without it, parts (a) and (b) sit unconnected.
2. Part (d) requires a substitution that is not signposted. Once $c$ is introduced, the equation in (c) becomes a quadratic, and the double-angle identity has to be applied *before* substituting, not after.

The elegant feature is that the answer is a surd involving $\sqrt5$ — the golden ratio — emerging from a purely algebraic root-of-unity argument. A candidate who sketches the five roots on a unit circle will see why $\sqrt5$ appears: the regular pentagon is built from it.

Classic wrong turns: assuming $\alpha^{4}=\alpha^{5}\alpha^{-1}$ is something other than $\alpha^{-1}$; using degrees inside an exponent written in terms of $\pi$; and choosing the negative root in (d) because $\cos(4\pi/5)$ is negative (it is the *other* cosine that is negative, not $c$).

A further wrong turn is to apply the double-angle identity to the wrong angle, expanding $\cos(4\pi/5)$ as $2\cos^{2}(4\pi/5)-1$; this is true but circular, leaving an equation in the quantity sought one step higher. A related slip is to drop the sign in $\cos(4\pi/5)=-\cos(\pi/5)$, which turns the quadratic into one with a spurious positive root.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: Rational functions; composite and self-inverse functions
questions.question:
A function $f$ is defined by

$$f(x)=\frac{3x+k}{x-3},\qquad x\neq3,\quad k\in\mathbb{R}.$$

(a)

Find an expression for $f(f(x))$, giving your answer in its simplest form.

[5]

(b)

Hence state the set of values of $k$ for which $f$ is self-inverse.

[2]

(c)

Show that when $k=-9$ the function $f$ is not self-inverse, and explain why.

[3]

(d)

Now let $k=7$. Find the coordinates of the points where the graph of $y=f(x)$ intersects the line $y=x$, and hence state what these points show about the graph.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Substitute $f(x)$ into itself:

$$f(f(x))=\frac{3\!\left(\dfrac{3x+k}{x-3}\right)+k}{\dfrac{3x+k}{x-3}-3}$$ (M1)

Multiply numerator and denominator by $(x-3)$:

$$=\frac{3(3x+k)+k(x-3)}{(3x+k)-3(x-3)}$$ (M1)

$$=\frac{9x+3k+kx-3k}{3x+k-3x+9}=\frac{x(9+k)}{k+9}$$ (A1)(A1)

$$f(f(x))=x,\qquad\text{provided }k\neq-9.$$ (A1)

Note the domain condition: the composite is defined only where $f(x)\neq3$, and solving $\dfrac{3x+k}{x-3}\neq3$ again gives $k\neq-9$. So the value that cancels the algebra is the same value that removes the composite's domain.

(b) A function is self-inverse when $f(f(x))=x$ (equivalently $f^{-1}=f$). From (a) this holds for every real $k$ except $k=-9$. (A1)(A1)

So: $f$ is self-inverse for all $k\in\mathbb{R},\ k\neq-9$.

(c) When $k=-9$:

$$f(x)=\frac{3x-9}{x-3}=\frac{3(x-3)}{x-3}=3\qquad(x\neq3)$$ (M1)(A1)

The function is then the constant function $f(x)=3$ on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{3\}$. It is not one-to-one (every input gives the same output), so no inverse function exists and in particular $f$ is not self-inverse. (R1)

Note that (a) also fails to give $x$ here: $\dfrac{x(9+k)}{k+9}=\dfrac{0}{0}$, which is undefined.

(d) Solve $f(x)=x$:

$$\frac{3x+7}{x-3}=x\ \Rightarrow\ 3x+7=x^{2}-3x\ \Rightarrow\ x^{2}-6x-7=0$$ (M1)

$$\Rightarrow\ (x-7)(x+1)=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=7\ \text{or}\ x=-1$$ (A1)

Check: $f(7)=\dfrac{21+7}{4}=7$ and $f(-1)=\dfrac{-3+7}{-4}=-1$. The points are $(7,\,7)$ and $(-1,-1)$. (A1)

Since $f$ is self-inverse (from (b), with $k=7\neq-9$), the graph of $y=f(x)$ is its own reflection in the line $y=x$; these two points are the fixed points — the points where the graph meets its own axis of symmetry. (R1)
questions.explanation:
The whole question turns on a piece of algebra that looks as though it should depend on $k$ and does not.

In part (a) the numerator simplifies to $x(9+k)$ and the denominator to $(k+9)$ — the same factor — so $f(f(x))=x$ for every $k$. Students rarely believe this on the first pass: they expect a messy expression and either stop early or make an algebraic slip that reintroduces a spurious $k$-dependence. The point is structural: for any Möbius map $f(x)=\dfrac{ax+b}{cx+d}$, self-inverse is equivalent to $a+d=0$, and here $a+d=3+(-3)=0$ regardless of $k$.

Part (c) is the trap. At $k=-9$ the algebra in (a) collapses to $0/0$, which is exactly the signal that something has gone wrong with the function rather than with the working. The constant function $f(x)=3$ is the degenerate case: it is not one-to-one, so it has no inverse at all — and this is the single value the 'for all $k$' claim must exclude.

Part (d) converts the algebra into geometry. A self-inverse graph is symmetric about $y=x$, so any fixed point must lie *on* that line, and finding them reduces to solving $f(x)=x$.

Classic wrong turns: cancelling $(x-3)$ before clearing the compound denominator; concluding 'self-inverse for all $k$' without testing the degenerate case; and in (d), solving $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$ (an identity here) instead of $f(x)=x$.

One more classic wrong turn is to treat the domain as incidental. Writing $f(f(x))=x$ for all real $x$ assumes $x=3$ is the only excluded input; the composite is defined only where $f(x)\neq3$, and at $k=-9$ that fails for every $x$, so the composite is empty rather than the identity. A candidate who inverts at $k=-9$ by the swap-and-solve route finds the equation collapse to $x=3$, and may mistake that for an inverse.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: Lines and planes in three dimensions
questions.question:
Two straight lines are given by

$$L_{1}:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
L_{2}:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix},\qquad s,\,t\in\mathbb{R}.$$

(a)

Show that $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are skew.

[4]

(b)

Find the acute angle between $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$.

[3]

(c)

Find the equation of the plane $\Pi$ that contains $L_{1}$ and is parallel to $L_{2}$, giving your answer in the form $\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=d$.

[4]

(d)

Hence find the shortest distance between $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Direction vectors: $\mathbf{d}_{1}=(2,-1,1)$, $\mathbf{d}_{2}=(1,1,-2)$.

$\mathbf{d}_{1}$ is not a scalar multiple of $\mathbf{d}_{2}$, so the lines are not parallel. (A1)

At an intersection:

$$1+2s=4+t\ \ (1),\qquad 2-s=1+t\ \ (2),\qquad 3+s=-2t\ \ (3)$$ (M1)

From (2): $t=1-s$. Substituting into (1): $1+2s=4+1-s\Rightarrow3s=4\Rightarrow s=\dfrac43$, so $t=-\dfrac13$. (A1)

Check in (3): LHS $=3+\dfrac43=\dfrac{13}{3}$; RHS $=-2\!\left(-\dfrac13\right)=\dfrac23$. Since $\dfrac{13}{3}\neq\dfrac23$, the equations are inconsistent and the lines do not intersect. (R1)

Not parallel and not intersecting $\Rightarrow$ skew.

(b)

$$\mathbf{d}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{d}_{2}=2(1)+(-1)(1)+1(-2)=2-1-2=-1$$ (M1)

$$|\mathbf{d}_{1}|=\sqrt{4+1+1}=\sqrt6,\qquad|\mathbf{d}_{2}|=\sqrt{1+1+4}=\sqrt6$$

$$\cos\theta=\frac{|\mathbf{d}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{d}_{2}|}{|\mathbf{d}_{1}||\mathbf{d}_{2}|}=\frac{1}{6}$$ (A1)

$$\theta=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac16\right)=80.4^{\circ}\ (1\ \text{d.p.})$$ (A1)

(c) $\Pi$ contains $\mathbf{d}_{1}$ and is parallel to $\mathbf{d}_{2}$, so its normal is

$$\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{d}_{1}\times\mathbf{d}_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}(-1)(-2)-(1)(1)\\(1)(1)-(2)(-2)\\(2)(1)-(-1)(1)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\5\\3\end{pmatrix}$$ (M1)(A1)

(Check: $\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}_{1}=2-5+3=0$ and $\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}_{2}=1+5-6=0$.)

$\Pi$ passes through $(1,2,3)$ on $L_{1}$, so

$$\mathbf{r}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}1\\5\\3\end{pmatrix}=1(1)+2(5)+3(3)=20$$ (M1)(A1)

$$\boxed{\ \mathbf{r}\cdot(1,\,5,\,3)=20\ }\qquad(\text{i.e. }x+5y+3z=20)$$

(d) Since $L_{2}$ is parallel to $\Pi$ and does not lie in it (its point $(4,1,0)$ gives $4+5+0=9\neq20$), the shortest distance between the skew lines is the perpendicular distance from $L_{2}$ to $\Pi$. (M1)

$$\text{distance}=\frac{|9-20|}{\sqrt{1^{2}+5^{2}+3^{2}}}=\frac{11}{\sqrt{35}}$$ (A1)

$$=\frac{11}{5.916}=1.86\ \text{units}\ (3\ \text{s.f.})$$ (A1)
questions.explanation:
The individual techniques here are standard; the difficulty is that part (d) has no obvious starting point unless you have deliberately built the plane in part (c) as a tool.

The idea that unlocks it: if you construct the unique plane that contains one line and is parallel to the other, then the second line lies at a *constant* perpendicular distance from that plane, and that constant is the shortest distance between the lines. Students who do not make this connection usually try to minimise $|\mathbf{r}_1(s)-\mathbf{r}_2(t)|$ directly — a two-variable minimisation that is possible but slow and error-prone without technology (and this is a no-technology paper).

Two smaller traps:

  • In (a), solving the first two component equations always produces values of $s$ and $t$; the question is only settled by substituting into the *third*. Candidates who stop after two equations will happily conclude 'they intersect'.
  • In (c) the normal must be perpendicular to *both* directions. Using $\mathbf{d}_1$ or $\mathbf{d}_2$ as the normal, or averaging them, are both common and both wrong.

The numbers were chosen so the arithmetic stays clean: the two direction vectors have equal magnitude $\sqrt6$, and the cross product gives a small-integer normal.

Classic wrong turns: using $\mathbf{d}_1\cdot\mathbf{d}_2$ without the modulus; omitting the check in (a); and in (d), computing the distance from a point on $L_1$ (which lies *in* the plane and so gives zero).

Two further wrong turns are worth naming. In (c), substituting the point $(4,1,0)$ from $L_{2}$ rather than $(1,2,3)$ from $L_{1}$ gives the parallel plane $x+5y+3z=9$, so every later distance is measured from the wrong reference. In (d), treating the two given points as the closest points and quoting $\sqrt{19}$ is the commonest numerical error.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 4.13 Bayes' theorem with two screening tests that are correlated given the disease status
questions.question:
A rare condition affects $0.8\%$ of a population. Two screening tests, $A$ and $B$, are
available. Test $A$ has sensitivity $0.95$ (that is, $\mathrm{P}(A^{+} \mid D) = 0.95$) and
false positive rate $0.04$ (that is, $\mathrm{P}(A^{+} \mid \overline{D}) = 0.04$), where $D$
denotes having the condition.

Test $B$ probes the same biomarker as test $A$, so the two results are correlated even among
people with the same disease status. Trial data for test $B$ are reported twice: once for the
whole population, and once for the subgroup who tested positive on test $A$.

$$\begin{array}{l|cc}
& \mathrm{P}(B^{+} \mid D) & \mathrm{P}(B^{+} \mid \overline{D}) \\ \hline
\text{whole population} & 0.86 & 0.18 \\
\text{subgroup with } A^{+} & 0.90 & 0.15
\end{array}$$

A person is selected at random, tests positive on test $A$, and is then given test $B$, on
which they also test positive.

(a) Find the probability that the person has the condition given the positive result on test
$A$ alone. \tag{3}

(b) State, with a reason, which row of the table is the appropriate one to use when combining
the two results. \tag{3}

(c) Calculate the probability that the person has the condition given that both tests are
positive. \tag{5}

(d) Explain why using the other row of the table gives a different answer. \tag{3}

(a)

Find the probability that the person has the condition given the positive result on test $A$ alone.

[3]

(b)

State, with a reason, which row of the table is the appropriate one to use.

[3]

(c)

Calculate $\mathrm{P}(D \mid A^{+} \cap B^{+})$.

[5]

(d)

Explain why using the other row of the table gives a different answer.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) By Bayes' theorem,

$$\mathrm{P}(D \mid A^{+}) = \frac{\mathrm{P}(D)\mathrm{P}(A^{+} \mid D)}
{\mathrm{P}(D)\mathrm{P}(A^{+} \mid D) + \mathrm{P}(\overline{D})\mathrm{P}(A^{+} \mid \overline{D})}
\tag{M1}$$

With $\mathrm{P}(D) = 0.008$ and $\mathrm{P}(\overline{D}) = 0.992$,

$$\mathrm{P}(D \mid A^{+}) = \frac{0.008 \times 0.95}{0.008 \times 0.95 + 0.992 \times 0.04}
= \frac{0.0076}{0.0076 + 0.03968} = \frac{0.0076}{0.04728} = 0.1607 \text{ (4 s.f.)} \tag{A1}$$

So a single positive result leaves the probability at about $16.1\%$ (A1) — still far more
likely than not that the person does *not* have the condition, because the condition is rare.

(b) The subgroup row, $\mathrm{P}(B^{+} \mid D) = 0.90$ and
$\mathrm{P}(B^{+} \mid \overline{D}) = 0.15$, is the appropriate one (A1). The reason is that
the relevant likelihoods are conditional on what is already known, namely that the person
tested positive on $A$ (R1): the quantity needed in part (c) is
$\mathrm{P}(B^{+} \mid A^{+} \cap D)$, not $\mathrm{P}(B^{+} \mid D)$ (A1). The population
row averages over people who tested negative on $A$, and those people are never given test
$B$.

(c) Applying Bayes' theorem with the two pieces of evidence,

$$\mathrm{P}(D \mid A^{+} \cap B^{+}) =
\frac{\mathrm{P}(D)\mathrm{P}(A^{+} \mid D)\mathrm{P}(B^{+} \mid A^{+} \cap D)}
{\mathrm{P}(D)\mathrm{P}(A^{+} \mid D)\mathrm{P}(B^{+} \mid A^{+} \cap D)
+ \mathrm{P}(\overline{D})\mathrm{P}(A^{+} \mid \overline{D})\mathrm{P}(B^{+} \mid A^{+} \cap \overline{D})}
\tag{M1}$$

Substituting the subgroup row (M1),

$$= \frac{0.008 \times 0.95 \times 0.90}{0.008 \times 0.95 \times 0.90 + 0.992 \times 0.04 \times 0.15}
= \frac{0.00684}{0.00684 + 0.005952} = \frac{0.00684}{0.012792} \tag{A1}$$

$$= 0.535 \text{ (3 s.f.)} \tag{A1}$$

Two positive results therefore raise the probability from about $16\%$ to about $53\%$ — a
substantial improvement, but still short of even odds (A1). Note that the two tests are *not*
treated as unconditionally independent: the subgroup figures already incorporate the
dependence between them.

(d) Using the population row instead gives

$$\frac{0.008 \times 0.95 \times 0.86}{0.008 \times 0.95 \times 0.86 + 0.992 \times 0.04 \times 0.18}
= \frac{0.006536}{0.006536 + 0.0071424} = 0.478 \text{ (3 s.f.)} \tag{A1}$$

which is about $5.7$ percentage points lower than the correct value (A1). The two rows differ
because the tests probe the same biomarker, so their outcomes are correlated even after the
disease status is fixed (R1). The subgroup with $A^{+}$ is not a random sample of the
population: selecting on a positive result from $A$ enriches it for people in whom the
biomarker is easy to detect, and test $B$ performs differently in that group. Using the
population figures tacitly assumes conditional independence of $A$ and $B$ given $D$, and that
assumption is exactly what the stem rules out.
questions.explanation:
The item is built on a distinction that is easy to state and easy to lose track of: the
accuracy of a test measured on a population, and the accuracy of the same test measured on the
subgroup who actually get it.

A candidate who has met two-stage screening before will reach for the pattern
$\mathrm{P}(D)\mathrm{P}(A^{+} \mid D)\mathrm{P}(B^{+} \mid D)$ in the numerator, because that
is what conditional independence looks like. Here that pattern is wrong twice over. It is
wrong as stated, because the likelihood needed is conditional on $A^{+}$ as well as on $D$; and
the number it tempts the candidate to substitute, $0.86$, is a population figure that has
already averaged over the people who never took test $B$.

The prevalence is doing quiet work throughout. Because only $0.8\%$ of the population has the
condition, the $4\%$ false positive rate on test $A$ generates $0.03968$ in the denominator
against $0.0076$ in the numerator — more than five times as much. A single positive test
therefore moves the probability only from $0.8\%$ to $16.1\%$, and even two positive tests
leave it at $53\%$. Candidates routinely find this counter-intuitive, and it is the reason the
item quotes a rare condition rather than a common one: the arithmetic has to fight the
prevalence, and the fight is the point.

Part (d) is where the two rows are reconciled. The reason they differ is that the tests are
correlated conditional on $D$, which is a physical claim about what they measure, not a
statistical technicality. Two tests for the same biomarker will tend to agree with each other
for reasons that have nothing to do with the disease, and that residual agreement means the
second test carries less fresh information than its headline accuracy suggests. Selecting on
$A^{+}$ makes the correlation visible as a difference between the two rows.

The $5.7$ percentage point gap between $0.478$ and $0.535$ is not a rounding artefact, and it
is large enough to matter in the setting the question describes: it is the difference between
a clinician who treats and one who does not.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 3.17 Shortest distance from a point to a line segment, where the perpendicular foot falls outside the segment
questions.question:
A monitoring cable is stretched taut between two pylons. Relative to axes measured in
metres, with the $z$-axis vertical, the ends of the cable are at $A(0,\, 2,\, 1)$ and
$B(4,\, 2,\, 4)$. A drone hovers at $P(7,\, 6,\, 7)$ and a second drone hovers at
$Q(1,\, 6,\, 2)$.

(a) Find a vector equation of the infinite line passing through $A$ and $B$. \tag{3}

(b) Find the value of the parameter $t$ at which the point of this line closest to $P$
occurs. \tag{3}

(c) Hence find the shortest distance from $P$ to the cable. \tag{5}

(d) Show that for the drone at $Q$ the closest point of the infinite line does lie on the
cable, and find the shortest distance from $Q$ to the cable. \tag{3}

(a)

Find a vector equation of the infinite line through $A$ and $B$.

[3]

(b)

Find the value of $t$ at which the point of this line closest to $P$ occurs.

[3]

(c)

Hence find the shortest distance from $P$ to the cable.

[5]

(d)

Show that for $Q$ the closest point lies on the cable, and find the shortest distance from $Q$ to the cable.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) $\overrightarrow{AB} = (4-0,\, 2-2,\, 4-1) = (4,\, 0,\, 3)$ (A1), so a vector equation of
the line is

$$\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}
+ t\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad t \in \mathbb{R} \tag{M1}$$

The cable itself is the portion with $0 \le t \le 1$ (A1). This restriction is the one that
matters later and it is worth stating explicitly at the start.

(b) Let $X$ be the point of the line with parameter $t$. Then
$\overrightarrow{AX} = t(4,0,3)$ and $\overrightarrow{AP} = (7, 4, 6)$ (A1). At the closest
point, $\overrightarrow{XP}$ is perpendicular to the direction of the line (M1), so

$$(\overrightarrow{AP} - t\overrightarrow{AB}) \cdot \overrightarrow{AB} = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t = \frac{\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}}
{\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}} \tag{M1}$$

Now $\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB} = 7(4) + 4(0) + 6(3) = 28 + 18 = 46$ and
$\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB} = 16 + 0 + 9 = 25$, so $t = \frac{46}{25} = 1.84$
(A1).

(c) Since $t = 1.84 > 1$, the closest point of the *infinite line* lies beyond $B$, on the
extension of the cable rather than on the cable itself (A1). The constrained minimum over
$0 \le t \le 1$ is therefore attained at an endpoint (R1), and because the parameter is
already past the end, that endpoint is $B$. Hence the shortest distance from $P$ to the cable
is simply $|BP|$ (M1):

$$\overrightarrow{BP} = (7-4,\, 6-2,\, 7-4) = (3,\, 4,\, 3) \tag{A1}$$

$$|BP| = \sqrt{3^{2} + 4^{2} + 3^{2}} = \sqrt{34} = 5.83 \text{ m (3 s.f.)} \tag{A1}$$

For comparison, the perpendicular distance to the infinite line is
$\frac{|\overrightarrow{AP} \times \overrightarrow{AB}|}{|\overrightarrow{AB}|}
= \frac{\sqrt{409}}{5} = 4.04$ m, which is $31\%$ too small — and is the answer a candidate
who never checks where the foot lands will give.

(d) $\overrightarrow{AQ} = (1, 4, 1)$ (A1), so
$\overrightarrow{AQ}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB} = 1(4) + 4(0) + 1(3) = 7$ and
$t = \frac{7}{25} = 0.28$ (A1). Since $0 \le 0.28 \le 1$, the closest point of the infinite
line does lie on the cable, so the perpendicular distance formula applies directly:

$$\overrightarrow{AQ} \times \overrightarrow{AB} = (12,\, 3,\, -16), \qquad
|\overrightarrow{AQ} \times \overrightarrow{AB}| = \sqrt{144 + 9 + 256} = \sqrt{401}$$

$$d = \frac{\sqrt{401}}{5} = 4.01 \text{ m (3 s.f.)} \tag{A1}$$
questions.explanation:
The formula for the distance from a point to a line is one of the most reliably remembered
results in the vectors topic, and it is quietly the wrong formula here — not because it is
wrong in general, but because it answers a question that was not asked. It gives the distance
to the infinite line; the cable is a segment.

The distinction only matters when the perpendicular foot falls outside the segment, and the
way to find out is to compute the parameter $t$ and look at it. Here $t = 1.84$, so the foot
sits well past $B$. Once that is known, the geometry changes character: on a closed interval,
a minimum that is not attained at an interior stationary point is attained at an endpoint, and
there is nothing left to differentiate. The distance is $|BP|$.

This is the general shape of a constrained optimisation. The unconstrained minimum is
stationary; the constrained minimum is stationary only if the constraint happens not to bind,
and when it does bind the minimum sits on the boundary and the stationarity condition simply
fails. Candidates meet this idea in one-variable calculus as "check the endpoints", meet it
again in linear programming as a vertex solution, and rarely connect the two. The cable
question is the same idea in vector form.

Part (d) is not decoration. A candidate who has just decided in (c) that the foot lands
outside might reasonably start assuming that always happens, and the second drone is there to
disconfirm it: $t = 0.28$, comfortably inside, and the perpendicular formula applies. Being
asked to handle both cases in one item is what forces the check to become a habit rather than
a one-off insight.

Numerically, the error is large enough to matter. The perpendicular distance is
$\frac{\sqrt{409}}{5} \approx 4.04$ m and the true distance is $\sqrt{34} \approx 5.83$ m. In
the setting the question describes — a drone near a cable — a $31\%$ understatement of a
clearance is the difference between a safe separation and a collision.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 4.9 linear combinations of independent normal variables; scaling one observation is not the same as summing four
questions.question:
The mass, $X$ grams, of a bag of flour from a production line is normally distributed with
mean $1000$ and standard deviation $12$. Bags are filled independently.

A quality-control procedure takes a random sample of four bags and weighs them together.
Let $S$ be the total mass of the four bags.

(a) State the distribution of $S$, giving its mean and standard deviation. \tag{3}

(b) Find $\mathrm{P}(S > 4040)$. \tag{3}

(c) A second, cheaper procedure weighs a single bag and multiplies the reading by $4$,
giving $T = 4X$. Show that $T$ has the same mean as $S$ but a different standard deviation,
and find $\mathrm{P}(T > 4040)$. \tag{4}

(d) Determine which of the two probabilities is the correct one to use for the total mass of
four bags, and explain why the two procedures agree about the mean but differ so sharply about
the tail. \tag{4}

(a)

State the distribution of $S$, giving its mean and standard deviation.

[3]

(b)

Find the probability that the total mass of the four bags exceeds $4040$ grams.

[3]

(c)

Show that $T = 4X$ has the same mean as $S$ but a different standard deviation, and find $\mathrm{P}(T > 4040)$.

[4]

(d)

Determine which probability is correct for the total mass of four bags, and explain why the two procedures agree about the mean but differ about the tail.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) $S = X_1 + X_2 + X_3 + X_4$ where the $X_i$ are independent copies of $X$ (M1). A
linear combination of independent normal variables is normal, so

$$\mathrm{E}(S) = 4 \times 1000 = 4000, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(S) = 4 \times 12^{2} = 4 \times 144 = 576
\tag{A1}$$

$$S \sim \mathrm{N}(4000,\, 576), \qquad \sigma_S = \sqrt{576} = 24 \text{ g} \tag{A1}$$

Note that the standard deviation scales as $\sqrt{4} = 2$, not as $4$: variances add for
independent variables, standard deviations do not.

(b) Standardising (M1),

$$z = \frac{4040 - 4000}{24} = \frac{40}{24} = 1.6667 \tag{A1}$$

$$\mathrm{P}(S > 4040) = \mathrm{P}(Z > 1.6667) = 1 - 0.9522 = 0.0478 \text{ (3 s.f.)} \tag{A1}$$

(c) $T = 4X$ is a linear scaling of a single normal variable, so $T$ is normal with (M1)

$$\mathrm{E}(T) = 4 \times 1000 = 4000 \quad \text{— the same mean as } S \tag{A1}$$

$$\mathrm{Var}(T) = 4^{2} \times 12^{2} = 16 \times 144 = 2304, \qquad \sigma_T = \sqrt{2304} = 48 \text{ g}
\tag{A1}$$

which is twice $\sigma_S$. Standardising, $z = \frac{40}{48} = 0.8333$ and

$$\mathrm{P}(T > 4040) = \mathrm{P}(Z > 0.8333) = 1 - 0.7977 = 0.202 \text{ (3 s.f.)} \tag{A1}$$

(d) The correct probability for the total mass of four bags is the one from (b),
$\mathrm{P}(S > 4040) = 0.0478$ (A1), because the total really is a sum of four independent
random variables and $T$ is not that sum (R1). The two procedures agree about the mean
because expectation is linear and does not require independence:
$\mathrm{E}(X_1 + X_2 + X_3 + X_4) = 4\mathrm{E}(X) = \mathrm{E}(4X)$ (A1). They differ about
the tail because variance is not linear in the same way: for a sum of independent variables
the variances add, giving $4\sigma^2$, whereas scaling a single observation multiplies the
variance by $4^{2} = 16$, giving $16\sigma^{2}$ (R1). The single-bag procedure therefore
inflates the spread by a factor of $2$ and overstates the probability of an extreme total by a
factor of about $4.2$. Averaging four independent measurements cancels some of the noise;
multiplying one measurement by four amplifies it.
questions.explanation:
The pair of procedures is chosen so that every obvious check passes on both of them. Both
are unbiased: $\mathrm{E}(S) = \mathrm{E}(T) = 4000$. Both are normal. Both are measured in
grams. A candidate who verifies only that the two methods "give the same answer on average"
will conclude that they are equivalent, and will then use whichever is more convenient —
which, unfortunately, is the wrong one, because $T$ needs only one weighing.

The difference is entirely in the spread, and it comes from one structural fact: the four bags
are independent. Independence is what allows variances to add, so
$\mathrm{Var}(S) = \sigma^2 + \sigma^2 + \sigma^2 + \sigma^2 = 4\sigma^2$ and
$\sigma_S = 2\sigma = 24$. The cheap procedure has no independence to exploit. It takes one
observation and stretches it, and stretching by a factor of $4$ multiplies the variance by
$4^2 = 16$, so $\sigma_T = 4\sigma = 48$.

The $\sqrt{n}$ versus $n$ distinction is the single most useful idea in the item. Summing $n$
independent measurements grows the standard deviation like $\sqrt{n}$; scaling one measurement
by $n$ grows it like $n$. For $n = 4$ those differ by a factor of $2$, and because the normal
tail is steep near two standard deviations, a factor of $2$ in the standard deviation moves the
tail probability by a factor of about $4.2$ — from $4.8\%$ to $20\%$.

That is why the wrong answer is dangerous rather than merely wrong. It is not a small
misestimate; it says an event is more than four times as likely as it is. In a quality-control
setting the practical consequence is that a line which is performing perfectly will appear to
trip the alarm on roughly one inspection in five.

The general lesson transfers well beyond this question: whenever a model replaces an average
of several independent quantities by a scaled version of one of them, the mean survives and
the variance does not. Checking the mean is not a check at all.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 5.11 The signed integral of an odd function over a symmetric interval vanishes while the geometric area between the curve and the axis does not, and the two lobes of f(x) = x^3 - a^2 x are exactly equal in magnitude
questions.question:
Let $a$ be a positive constant and define
$$f(x) = x^{3} - a^{2}x.$$
The function is being used to model a shallow channel cut across a strip of land, with $x$ measured in metres from the centre line and $f(x)$ the depth of the channel in metres, taken as positive upwards. Two different quantities are wanted from the same curve: the signed integral, which is what an instrument that accumulates the profile as it is driven along would record, and the geometric area between the curve and the $x$-axis, which is what a surveyor who measures the visible cross-section would report. The figure shows the case $a = 2$.

(a)

Show that $f$ is an odd function and hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx$ without performing any integration.

[3]

(b)

Determine the geometric area of the region enclosed between the curve, the $x$-axis and the lines $x = -a$ and $x = a$, giving your answer in terms of $a$.

[4]

(c)

The geometric area is found to be $8$ square metres. Determine the value of $a$ and the coordinates of the two turning points of the curve for that value of $a$.

[4]

(d)

Explain why the signed integral in part (a) is zero while the geometric area in part (b) is not, and state what the instrument described in the question would record as it is driven from $x = -a$ to $x = a$.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The function is odd if $f(-x) = -f(x)$ for every $x$. Here
$$f(-x) = (-x)^{3} - a^{2}(-x) = -x^{3} + a^{2}x = -(x^{3} - a^{2}x) = -f(x),$$
so $f$ is odd (M1)(A1). For an odd function the integral over a symmetric interval vanishes, because the substitution $u = -x$ maps the interval onto itself and reverses the sign:
$$\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{a}\bigl(f(x) + f(-x)\bigr)dx = \int_{0}^{a}\bigl(f(x) - f(x)\bigr)dx = 0 \;(A1).$$
The cancellation is exact, not approximate, and it holds for every value of $a$.
(b) The curve meets the axis where $x(x^{2} - a^{2}) = 0$, that is at $x = -a$, $x = 0$ and $x = a$ (M1). On $0 < x < a$ the factor $x^{2} - a^{2}$ is negative, so $f(x) < 0$ and the curve lies below the axis; on $-a < x < 0$ the two factors are both negative, so $f(x) > 0$ and the curve lies above it (A1). The geometric area therefore requires the absolute value of $f$, and by the odd symmetry the two lobes have equal area, so
$$\text{area} = 2\int_{0}^{a}\bigl(a^{2}x - x^{3}\bigr)dx = 2\left[\frac{a^{2}x^{2}}{2} - \frac{x^{4}}{4}\right]_{0}^{a} = 2\left(\frac{a^{4}}{2} - \frac{a^{4}}{4}\right) = 2\cdot\frac{a^{4}}{4} = \frac{a^{4}}{2} \;(M1)(A1).$$
With $a = 2$ this is $16/2 = 8$ square metres (A1). Note that the two lobes have equal area precisely because $f$ is odd; the equal magnitudes are the same fact that made the signed integral vanish.
(c) Setting $a^{4}/2 = 8$ gives $a^{4} = 16$, and since $a > 0$, $a = 2$ (M1)(A1). The turning points satisfy $f'(x) = 3x^{2} - a^{2} = 0$, so
$$x = \pm\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}} = \pm\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = \pm 1.1547\ldots \;(A1).$$Substituting into $f$ gives $f\!\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = \frac{a^{3}}{3\sqrt{3}} - \frac{a^{3}}{\sqrt{3}} = -\frac{2a^{3}}{3\sqrt{3}}$, which for $a = 2$ is $-3.0792\ldots$ (A1). By the odd symmetry the other turning point is its reflection, so the two points are
$$\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}},\ -\frac{16}{3\sqrt{3}}\right) \approx (1.155,\ -3.079) \quad\text{and}\quad \left(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}},\ \frac{16}{3\sqrt{3}}\right) \approx (-1.155,\ 3.079) \;(A1).$$
(d) The signed integral adds the two lobes with their signs attached, and because the lobes are mirror images through the origin the positive contribution and the negative contribution are equal in magnitude, so their sum is zero (A1). The geometric area adds the magnitudes, and a magnitude cannot cancel (A1). The instrument accumulates the signed value as it is driven along, so it rises while it crosses the positive lobe, falls back through zero at the centre, and returns to exactly zero at $x = a$; its final reading is zero even though it has been recording a non-zero depth the whole way (A1). A surveyor reading the same profile with a tape would report $8$ square metres, and the two answers are both correct because they answer different questions.
questions.explanation:
There is one idea in this item and it is worth being precise about, because it is the commonest confusion in the whole of integration: a definite integral is a signed accumulation and an area is not. The two coincide only when the curve stays on one side of the axis.

Here the curve crosses the axis twice inside the interval of integration, so the two lobes contribute with opposite signs. Because the function is odd, the two lobes are congruent, and the cancellation is complete. That completeness is what makes the item sharp. If the cancellation were partial the candidate would be left with a non-zero residue and might notice that it did not look like an area; because it is total, the answer zero looks like a clean result, and a clean result is easy to accept. The figure is drawn to make the cancellation visible: the shaded regions are clearly not empty, yet their signed sum is nothing.

Part (b) reverses the demand. The same symmetry that made the integral vanish now does the work of the calculation, because the two lobes have equal area, so one lobe can be computed and doubled. The integral of $a^{2}x - x^{3}$, which is the absolute value of $f$ on the positive half, is a routine polynomial integral and gives $a^{4}/4$; doubling gives $a^{4}/2$. A candidate who forgets the doubling answers $a^{4}/4$ and, worse, will still find $a = 2^{3/4}$ in part (c) and produce a consistent-looking but wrong pair of turning points.

Part (c) is where an assumption about where the extremum sits costs marks. The turning points of $x^{3} - a^{2}x$ are at $x = \pm a/\sqrt{3}$, which is about $\pm 0.577a$: well inside the interval, but not at any of the obvious places. A candidate who guesses $x = \pm 1$ for $a = 2$ obtains ordinates of $-3$ rather than $-3.079$, close enough to look plausible on a sketch and wrong on the page.

Part (d) is the conceptual close. The instrument described in the stem is a device that accumulates the signed profile, so it rises over the first lobe, falls back through zero, and finishes at zero. It has recorded a non-zero depth at almost every point and its total is still zero. Being able to say that in words is the evidence that the candidate has separated the two notions rather than memorised two formulas.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 5.12 The integral of x to the power minus p on (0, 1]: convergence only for p < 1, the partial integral (1 - eps^(1-p))/(1 - p), and the failure of the power rule at p = 1 where the antiderivative is not defined at the lower limit
questions.question:
For a real constant $p$ define
$$I(p) = \int_{0}^{1} x^{-p}\,dx,$$
which for some values of $p$ is an improper integral, because the integrand $x^{-p} \to \infty$ as $x \to 0^{+}$ whenever $p > 0$. The integral is defined as the limit
$$I(p) = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^{+}}\int_{\varepsilon}^{1} x^{-p}\,dx$$
whenever that limit exists and is finite, and is said to diverge otherwise. The integrand has no upper bound near the lower limit, so the integral represents an area that is infinitely tall but only finitely wide, and whether that area is finite is the question. Answers should be given exactly, and the limit as $\varepsilon \to 0^{+}$ should be shown at each stage rather than asserted.

(a)

Show that for $p \ne 1$ and $0 < \varepsilon < 1$, $\displaystyle\int_{\varepsilon}^{1} x^{-p}\,dx = \frac{1 - \varepsilon^{1-p}}{1 - p}$.

[3]

(b)

Hence determine $I\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)$ and $I\!\left(\tfrac{3}{4}\right)$, showing the limit explicitly in each case.

[4]

(c)

Determine the set of real values of $p$ for which $I(p)$ converges, and give the value of the integral for those values of $p$. Justify the boundary of the set.

[4]

(d)

Explain what is wrong with applying the power rule directly to $p = 2$ and reporting $I(2) = -1$, and describe the behaviour of the partial integral as $\varepsilon \to 0^{+}$ in that case.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) For $p \ne 1$ the antiderivative of $x^{-p}$ is $\dfrac{x^{1-p}}{1 - p}$, so
$$\int_{\varepsilon}^{1} x^{-p}\,dx = \left[\frac{x^{1-p}}{1 - p}\right]_{\varepsilon}^{1} = \frac{1}{1 - p} - \frac{\varepsilon^{1-p}}{1 - p} = \frac{1 - \varepsilon^{1-p}}{1 - p} \;(M1)(A1).$$
The calculation is valid for every $p \ne 1$ and every $\varepsilon$ with $0 < \varepsilon < 1$, because the integrand is continuous on the closed interval $[\varepsilon, 1]$ and the fundamental theorem applies there (A1). Nothing has been assumed about the behaviour at $x = 0$; that is deferred to the limit.
(b) For $p = \tfrac{1}{2}$ the exponent is $1 - p = \tfrac{1}{2}$, so
$$\int_{\varepsilon}^{1} x^{-1/2}\,dx = \frac{1 - \varepsilon^{1/2}}{1/2} = 2\bigl(1 - \sqrt{\varepsilon}\bigr) \;(M1).$$
As $\varepsilon \to 0^{+}$ the term $\sqrt{\varepsilon} \to 0$, so the limit is $2$ and $I\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = 2$ (A1).
For $p = \tfrac{3}{4}$ the exponent is $1 - p = \tfrac{1}{4}$, so
$$\int_{\varepsilon}^{1} x^{-3/4}\,dx = \frac{1 - \varepsilon^{1/4}}{1/4} = 4\bigl(1 - \varepsilon^{1/4}\bigr) \;(M1),$$
and as $\varepsilon \to 0^{+}$ the term $\varepsilon^{1/4} \to 0$, giving $I\!\left(\tfrac{3}{4}\right) = 4$ (A1). In both cases the partial integral rises towards a finite value and stays below it.
(c) From part (a) the limit depends on the behaviour of $\varepsilon^{1-p}$ as $\varepsilon \to 0^{+}$, and there are three cases (M1).
If $p < 1$ then $1 - p > 0$, so $\varepsilon^{1-p} \to 0$ and $\dfrac{1 - \varepsilon^{1-p}}{1 - p} \to \dfrac{1}{1 - p}$. The integral converges and $I(p) = \dfrac{1}{1 - p}$ (A1).
If $p = 1$ the formula does not apply, and the partial integral must be computed separately: $\displaystyle\int_{\varepsilon}^{1}\frac{dx}{x} = -\ln\varepsilon$, which tends to $+\infty$ as $\varepsilon \to 0^{+}$ (A1). The integral diverges.
If $p > 1$ then $1 - p < 0$, so $\varepsilon^{1-p} = \varepsilon^{-(p-1)} = 1/\varepsilon^{\,p-1} \to +\infty$ as $\varepsilon \to 0^{+}$. Since $1 - p < 0$ as well, the quotient $\dfrac{1 - \varepsilon^{1-p}}{1 - p}$ tends to $+\infty$ (A1). The integral diverges.
So $I(p)$ converges exactly for $p < 1$, and for those values $I(p) = \dfrac{1}{1 - p}$. The boundary of the set is $p = 1$, where the two behaviours on either side -- a finite limit from below and divergence from above -- are separated.
(d) Applying the power rule to $p = 2$ gives the antiderivative $\dfrac{x^{-1}}{-1} = -\dfrac{1}{x}$, and substituting the limits formally gives $-1 - (-1/0)$, which involves division by zero (M1). The step that is illegitimate is the substitution of $x = 0$: the antiderivative $-\dfrac{1}{x}$ is not defined at the lower limit, so the fundamental theorem of calculus, which requires an antiderivative continuous on the whole interval of integration, does not apply (A1). The correct calculation uses the partial integral
$$\int_{\varepsilon}^{1} x^{-2}\,dx = \frac{1 - \varepsilon^{-1}}{-1} = \frac{1}{\varepsilon} - 1,$$
which grows without bound as $\varepsilon \to 0^{+}$: at $\varepsilon = 0.1$ it is $9$, at $\varepsilon = 0.01$ it is $99$, and at $\varepsilon = 0.001$ it is $999$ (A1). The integral diverges, and the reported value $-1$ is an artefact of evaluating a formula outside the range where it means anything.
questions.explanation:
The temptation in this question is to notice that the antiderivative has an elementary form and to treat the improper integral as a substitution problem. It is not one. The whole content of the item is the distinction between an antiderivative that exists on the open interval and an antiderivative that can be evaluated at both endpoints.

For $0 < p < 1$ the substitution works, and the reason it works is not luck. The exponent $1 - p$ is positive, so $\varepsilon^{1-p}$ goes to zero as $\varepsilon$ does: the partial integral approaches its limit from below and the contribution from the neighbourhood of the singularity vanishes. The integrand is unbounded, but it is integrable, and the total area under it is finite. This is the case that makes the infinite spike look harmless.

At $p = 1$ the formula breaks and the break is real. The integral of $1/x$ is a logarithm, and the logarithm diverges at zero. There is no cancellation and no finite limit. This is the boundary: on one side the spike is thin enough to have finite area and on the other it is not, and the dividing case is the one where the antiderivative is logarithmic.

For $p > 1$ the same formula is still algebraically correct as a partial integral, but now the exponent $1 - p$ is negative, so $\varepsilon^{1-p}$ blows up as $\varepsilon$ shrinks. The partial integral is $1/\varepsilon - 1$ for $p = 2$, and it grows without bound: ten, a hundred, a thousand. The formula $1/(1 - p) = -1$ is obtained by setting $\varepsilon = 0$ in an expression where that substitution is exactly what is forbidden. The negative sign is the tell, but it is a symptom; the error is the substitution.

The reason this matters beyond the exercise is that the same confusion appears whenever an integral is evaluated over a region where the integrand is singular. The safe habit is the one the question forces: write the integral from $\varepsilon$, integrate on the closed interval where the theorem applies, and then take the limit and see whether it exists. The formula is the last step, not the first.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 1.15 An induction whose step is valid only for indices above a threshold: n! > 3^n first holds at n = 7 because n = 6 falls short by nine, and the inductive step needs n > 2, so the base case must be chosen above that threshold rather than at the smallest index
questions.question:
Let $a_{n} = n!$ and $b_{n} = 3^{n}$ for positive integers $n$. The two sequences are compared below, and the comparison is then used to make a claim about the infinite series $\displaystyle\sum_{n \ge 1}\frac{3^{n}}{n!}$. Note that the inequality $n! > 3^{n}$ is not true for small $n$; it is the point of the question to establish exactly where it begins to hold, and to say why the proof must begin there and nowhere earlier.

(a)

Determine, by evaluating both $n!$ and $3^{n}$ at each integer from $1$ upwards, the smallest positive integer $N$ for which $n! > 3^{n}$ holds at $n = N$.

[2]

(b)

Prove by induction that $n! > 3^{n}$ for all integers $n \ge N$, stating precisely the inequality that your inductive step requires of $k$ and verifying that the base case satisfies it.

[5]

(c)

Explain why the induction cannot be started at $n = 3$ or at $n = 4$ even though the algebra of the inductive step is valid for every $k \ge 3$.

[3]

(d)

A student argues that because $n! > 3^{n}$ for $n \ge N$, every term of $\displaystyle\sum_{n \ge 1}\frac{3^{n}}{n!}$ is less than $1$, and the series therefore converges. Explain why this argument does not establish convergence, and determine by a valid test whether the series converges, giving the limit of the ratio of successive terms.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Evaluating both expressions from $n = 1$:
$$1! = 1 < 3, \quad 2! = 2 < 9, \quad 3! = 6 < 27, \quad 4! = 24 < 81, \quad 5! = 120 < 243, \quad 6! = 720 < 729, \quad 7! = 5040 > 2187 \;(M1).$$
At $n = 6$ the factorial falls short by $729 - 720 = 9$, which is the last failure, and the inequality first holds at $n = 7$. So $N = 7$ (A1).
(b) Claim: $n! > 3^{n}$ for every integer $n \ge 7$.
Base case $n = 7$: $7! = 5040$ and $3^{7} = 2187$, so $5040 > 2187$ and the claim holds (B1).
Inductive step. Assume for some integer $k \ge 7$ that $k! > 3^{k}$ (M1). Then
$$(k+1)! = (k+1)\cdot k! > (k+1)\cdot 3^{k} \;(A1).$$
The right-hand side exceeds $3^{k+1} = 3 \cdot 3^{k}$ exactly when $(k+1) > 3$, that is when $k > 2$ (A1). Since $k \ge 7$ certainly satisfies $k > 2$, the required inequality holds, and combining the two steps gives
$$(k+1)! > (k+1)\cdot 3^{k} > 3\cdot 3^{k} = 3^{k+1} \;(A1).$$
So the claim passes from $k$ to $k+1$ for every $k \ge 7$, and with the base case at $n = 7$ it holds for all $n \ge 7$ by induction (A1).
The inequality the step requires of $k$ is $k + 1 > 3$, and it is worth recording that this is the only place where the number $3$ in $3^{n}$ enters the proof in a way that constrains the index. Had the comparison been with $2^{n}$ the condition would have been $k + 1 > 2$, that is $k > 1$.
(c) The inductive step is valid for every $k \ge 3$, because that is exactly the range in which $k + 1 > 3$ (A1). Validity of the step is not enough on its own: an induction needs a true base case, and the step then propagates truth upwards from it. At $n = 3$ the claim reads $6 > 27$, which is false, and at $n = 4$ it reads $24 > 81$, which is also false (A1). Starting at either would be starting from a false statement, and a false statement can imply anything, so nothing would be proved. The base case must be chosen both above the threshold the step imposes and at an index where the claim is actually true; the smallest index satisfying both conditions is $N = 7$ (A1).
(d) The argument is invalid because the bound $3^{n}/n! < 1$ is uniform and says nothing about the size of the terms as $n$ grows. The harmonic series $\sum 1/n$ has every term less than $1$ and diverges, so a bound of this kind cannot establish convergence (A1).
A valid test is the ratio test. Writing $u_{n} = \dfrac{3^{n}}{n!}$,
$$\frac{u_{n+1}}{u_{n}} = \frac{3^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\cdot\frac{n!}{3^{n}} = \frac{3}{n+1} \;(M1),$$
so
$$\lim_{n \to \infty}\frac{u_{n+1}}{u_{n}} = \lim_{n \to \infty}\frac{3}{n+1} = 0 \;(A1).$$
Since $0 < 1$, the ratio test gives convergence (A1). The ratio is the quantity the inequality of part (b) cannot supply: it shows that successive terms shrink by a factor that itself tends to zero, which is far stronger than each term being less than one.
questions.explanation:
This item is about the two places an induction can fail, and it is constructed so that both are present at once.

The first place is the base case. A candidate who has learned induction as a template reaches for $n = 1$ without looking at whether the claim is true there. Here it is false at $n = 1$ through $n = 6$, and the last of those failures is uncomfortably close: $6! = 720$ against $3^{6} = 729$. A shortfall of nine is small enough that a candidate who rounds, or who estimates $6!$ as "about seven hundred", may well conclude that the inequality holds from $n = 6$. Evaluating both sides exactly is the only safe route, and it is why part (a) asks for the value at every integer rather than for a judgement.

The second place is the step, and this is the subtler of the two. The manipulation $(k+1)! = (k+1)k! > (k+1)3^{k}$ is correct for every $k$, and it is tempting to write the next inequality, $(k+1)3^{k} > 3^{k+1}$, as though it followed automatically. It does not: it is equivalent to $k + 1 > 3$. For $k = 1$ and $k = 2$ it is false, and a candidate who starts the induction at $n = 1$ or $n = 2$ is relying on a step that does not hold at the values being used. The item asks for that condition to be stated, which means the candidate has to notice that the comparison with $3^{n}$ imposes a threshold on the index at all. With $2^{n}$ the threshold would be $k > 1$; with $4^{n}$ it would be $k > 3$. The threshold is a property of the constant, and it is the reason the base case cannot simply be the smallest index for which the claim happens to be true.

Part (c) joins the two. The step is valid from $k = 3$ upwards, so an induction starting at $n = 3$ would propagate correctly if it could get started; but the claim is false at $n = 3$ and at $n = 4$, so there is nothing to propagate. The base case has to satisfy two conditions, not one, and part (c) exists to make the candidate say so.

Part (d) closes a loophole that a candidate might think the earlier parts opened. The inequality $n! > 3^{n}$ says that $3^{n}/n! < 1$ from $n = 7$ onwards. It is natural to read that as convergence, and it is wrong: the harmonic series is the standard counterexample, with every term below one and no finite sum. What the inequality does give is a bound, and a bound below one is not a rate. The ratio test supplies the rate, and the rate is $3/(n+1)$, which tends to zero -- far stronger than anything the inequality provides. The contrast between the two is the point of putting them in the same question.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 1.11 Partial fractions
questions.command_term: Show that, Hence, Write down, Determine
questions.question:
For each integer $n\geq1$, let $u_n=\dfrac{1}{n(n+1)(n+2)}$.

(a)

Show that $u_n$ can be written in the form $\dfrac{A}{n}+\dfrac{B}{n+1}+\dfrac{C}{n+2}$ and state the values of $A$, $B$ and $C$.

[3]

(b)

Hence show that $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}u_n=\dfrac14-\dfrac{1}{2(N+1)(N+2)}$ for every positive integer $N$.

[4]

(c)

Hence write down the value of the infinite sum $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}u_n$.

[2]

(d)

Hence determine the value of $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)}$.

[5]
questions.answer:
(a) Write $\dfrac{1}{n(n+1)(n+2)}=\dfrac{A}{n}+\dfrac{B}{n+1}+\dfrac{C}{n+2}$. Multiplying through by $n(n+1)(n+2)$ gives

$$1=A(n+1)(n+2)+Bn(n+2)+Cn(n+1).$$ (M1)

Setting $n=0$: $1=2A$, so $A=\tfrac12$. Setting $n=-1$: $1=(-1)(1)B$, so $B=-1$. Setting $n=-2$: $1=(-2)(-1)C$, so $C=\tfrac12$. (A1)(A1)

Hence $u_n=\dfrac{1}{2n}-\dfrac{1}{n+1}+\dfrac{1}{2(n+2)}$. (A1) *(AG)*

(b) The three-term form does not telescope cleanly, so regroup it. Note that

$$\frac{1}{n(n+1)}-\frac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)}=\frac{(n+2)-n}{n(n+1)(n+2)}=\frac{2}{n(n+1)(n+2)}.$$ (M1)

Therefore

$$u_n=\frac12\left(\frac{1}{n(n+1)}-\frac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)}\right),$$ (A1)

a difference of two consecutive values of $w_n=\dfrac{1}{n(n+1)}$. Summing,

$$\sum_{n=1}^{N}u_n=\frac12\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(w_n-w_{n+1}\right)=\frac12\left(w_1-w_{N+1}\right)$$ (M1)

$$=\frac12\left(\frac{1}{1\cdot2}-\frac{1}{(N+1)(N+2)}\right)=\frac14-\frac{1}{2(N+1)(N+2)}.$$ (A1) *(AG)*

(c) As $N\to\infty$ the fraction $\dfrac{1}{2(N+1)(N+2)}$ tends to $0$, so the tail disappears. (A1) Hence $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}u_n=\frac14$. (A1)

(d) Let $v_n=\dfrac{1}{n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)}$. Use the same device one order higher, taking the difference of two consecutive blocks of three factors:

$$\frac{1}{n(n+1)(n+2)}-\frac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)}=\frac{(n+3)-n}{n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)}=\frac{3}{n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)}.$$ (M1)

Hence $v_n=\dfrac13\left(\dfrac{1}{n(n+1)(n+2)}-\dfrac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)}\right)$. (A1) Summing from $n=1$ to $N$ telescopes to

$$\sum_{n=1}^{N}v_n=\frac13\left(\frac{1}{1\cdot2\cdot3}-\frac{1}{(N+1)(N+2)(N+3)}\right).$$ (M1)

As $N\to\infty$ the second term vanishes, so $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}v_n=\frac13\cdot\frac16=\frac{1}{18}$. (A1)(A1)

Edge-case checks. In (b), at $N=1$ the formula gives $\tfrac14-\tfrac1{12}=\tfrac16$, matching the single term $u_{1}=\tfrac16$. In (d), at $N=1$ it gives $\tfrac13\!\left(\tfrac16-\tfrac{1}{24}\right)=\tfrac1{24}=v_{1}$; only this first term survives as $N\to\infty$.
questions.explanation:
The question looks like a routine partial-fractions exercise, and part (a) is exactly that. The difficulty begins in part (b), and it is a difficulty of structure rather than of algebra.

The three-term decomposition produced in (a) is correct, but it is not the form in which the sum collapses. Summing $\frac{1}{2n}-\frac{1}{n+1}+\frac{1}{2(n+2)}$ from $n=1$ to $N$ does telescope, but three interleaved sequences have to be tracked and the boundary terms are easy to mis-assign. The intended observation is that the product $n(n+1)(n+2)$ can be split as a difference of two consecutive blocks, $\frac{1}{n(n+1)}-\frac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)}$. This is one quantity evaluated at $n$ and at $n+1$, so the sum over $n$ collapses at once to first term minus last term.

This is the lever. The student must construct a decomposition that part (a) did not ask for, and must recognise that a partial-fraction decomposition and a telescoping decomposition are not the same thing. Many candidates never make this distinction and grind through the three-term sum, usually losing a boundary term.

Part (d) tests whether the construction was understood or merely memorised. The four-factor denominator needs the same idea one order up: the difference of two consecutive blocks of three factors has numerator $3$, so the constant is $\tfrac13$, and the surviving first term is $\frac{1}{1\cdot2\cdot3}=\frac16$. A candidate who has memorised the answer $\frac14$ will reach for a similar-looking fraction and produce nonsense.

The classic wrong turns are: treating the three-term form as already telescoping and dropping the $n+2$ tail; forgetting that the first term is the only survivor as $N\to\infty$; and, in (d), reusing the constant $\tfrac12$ from part (b). A useful check is the general identity $\sum_{n\geq1}\frac{1}{n(n+1)\cdots(n+k)}=\frac{1}{k\cdot k!}$; for $k=2$ it gives $\frac14$ and for $k=3$ it gives $\frac{1}{18}$, both confirmed by the parts above.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: P3 extended problem: expected waiting times for patterns in a biased coin sequence
questions.question:
A biased coin is tossed repeatedly and independently. Each toss lands heads with probability $p$ and tails with probability $1 - p$, where $0 < p < 1$. For a given sequence of outcomes, the waiting time is the number of tosses needed to see that sequence for the first time. Let $E_{HH}$ and $E_{HT}$ denote the expected waiting times for the sequences $HH$ and $HT$ respectively.

(a)

By considering the two states 'no progress towards $HT$' and 'the last toss was $H$', show that
$$E_{HT} = \frac{1}{p\,(1-p)}.$$

[4]

(b)

By a similar argument with the two states 'no progress towards $HH$' and 'the last toss was $H$', show that
$$E_{HH} = \frac{1+p}{p^{2}}.$$

[4]

(c)

Hence show that $E_{HH} < E_{HT}$ if and only if $p > \dfrac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}$.

[3]

(d)

Taking $p = \dfrac{2}{3}$, calculate $E_{HH}$ and $E_{HT}$. By comparing the values of $E_{HH}$ and $E_{HT}$ at $p = \dfrac{1}{2}$, comment on the claim that the rarer of two equally long patterns always takes longer to appear.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Let $A$ be the expected number of further tosses needed from the state in which no progress towards $HT$ has been made, and let $B$ be the expected number of further tosses needed from the state in which the last toss was $H$ (M1).

From state $B$: one toss is made; a tail completes the pattern with probability $1-p$, and a head returns to state $B$ with probability $p$. Hence $B = 1 + p B + (1-p) \cdot 0$ (M1), so $(1-p)B = 1$ and $B = \dfrac{1}{1-p}$ (A1).

From state $A$: one toss is made; a head moves to state $B$ with probability $p$, and a tail leaves us in state $A$ with probability $1-p$. Hence $A = 1 + pB + (1-p)A$ (M1), so $pA = 1 + pB$ and $A = \dfrac{1}{p} + B = \dfrac{1}{p} + \dfrac{1}{1-p} = \dfrac{(1-p) + p}{p(1-p)} = \dfrac{1}{p(1-p)}$ (A1) (AG). Since we begin with no tosses made, $E_{HT} = A = \dfrac{1}{p(1-p)}$.

(b) Let $C$ be the expected number of further tosses from the state in which no progress towards $HH$ has been made, and let $D$ be the expected number of further tosses from the state in which the last toss was $H$ (M1).

From state $D$: one toss is made; a head completes the pattern with probability $p$, and a tail sends us back to state $C$ with probability $1-p$, because a tail destroys all progress. Hence $D = 1 + p \cdot 0 + (1-p)C$ (M1).

From state $C$: one toss is made; a head moves to state $D$ with probability $p$, and a tail leaves us in state $C$ with probability $1-p$. Hence $C = 1 + pD + (1-p)C$ (M1), so $pC = 1 + pD$ and $C = \dfrac{1}{p} + D$.

Substituting $D = 1 + (1-p)C$ into $C = \dfrac{1}{p} + D$ gives $C = \dfrac{1}{p} + 1 + (1-p)C$, so $pC = \dfrac{1}{p} + 1 = \dfrac{1+p}{p}$ and $C = \dfrac{1+p}{p^{2}}$ (A1) (AG). Since we begin with no tosses made, $E_{HH} = C = \dfrac{1+p}{p^{2}}$.

(c) The two expectations are equal when
$$\frac{1+p}{p^{2}} = \frac{1}{p(1-p)} \iff (1+p)(1-p) = p \iff 1 - p^{2} = p \iff p^{2} + p - 1 = 0$$ (M1).
The roots are $p = \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1+4}}{2} = \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}$, and since $0 < p < 1$ only $p = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2} \approx 0.6180$ is admissible (A1). To decide the direction, test $p = \dfrac{2}{3} > \dfrac{\sqrt5-1}{2}$: here $E_{HH} = 3.75$ and $E_{HT} = 4.5$, so $E_{HH} < E_{HT}$ (M1). Since the difference $E_{HH} - E_{HT}$ changes sign only at the single value found above, $E_{HH} < E_{HT}$ precisely for $p > \dfrac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$ (A1) (AG).

(d) At $p = \dfrac{2}{3}$ we have $1 - p = \dfrac{1}{3}$, so
$$E_{HH} = \frac{1 + \frac{2}{3}}{\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{2}} = \frac{\frac{5}{3}}{\frac{4}{9}} = \frac{5}{3} \times \frac{9}{4} = \frac{15}{4} = 3.75,$$ (M1)
$$E_{HT} = \frac{1}{\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{1}{3}} = \frac{1}{\frac{2}{9}} = \frac{9}{2} = 4.5$$ (A1).

At $p = \dfrac{1}{2}$ both patterns have probability $\dfrac{1}{4}$, yet $E_{HH} = \dfrac{1.5}{0.25} = 6$ while $E_{HT} = \dfrac{1}{0.25} = 4$ (A1). The claim is therefore false: two patterns of the same length and the same probability can have expected waiting times differing by 50%. What governs the waiting time is not how likely the pattern is but how much of a partial match survives a failure -- a tail destroys all progress towards $HH$, whereas for $HT$ a head simply leaves the state unchanged -- and this overlap structure is not visible in the pattern probabilities at all (AG).
questions.explanation:
The reason this problem is a trap rather than an exercise is that the intuition it defeats is a good intuition in almost every other setting. Usually, rarer events do take longer to occur, and here the two patterns have the same length, so it feels as though nothing else could distinguish them. The calculation shows that at $p = 1/2$ the two patterns are exactly equally likely -- probability $1/4$ each -- and yet one takes 6 tosses on average and the other takes 4. So the probability of the pattern is not the variable that governs the waiting time, and the student has to find the variable that does.

That variable is the pattern's self-overlap. When you are waiting for $HH$ and you have just seen one $H$, a tail destroys your progress entirely: you are back to having nothing, and you must see two heads in a row from scratch. When you are waiting for $HT$ and you have just seen one $H$, a head does not destroy your progress at all -- it leaves you in exactly the state you were already in, still needing one tail. That asymmetry is worth 50% of the expected time, and it is completely invisible in the two probabilities. The recurrences make the asymmetry explicit: in part (a) the failure branch returns to $B$, in part (b) it returns to $C$. Candidates who do not notice this will write the same recurrence twice and get the same answer twice.

Once both expressions are in hand, part (c) is a clean piece of algebra that produces the golden ratio. It is worth pausing on why the answer is a golden ratio and not, say, $1/2$: the condition $(1+p)(1-p) = p$ rearranges to $p^{2} + p - 1 = 0$, which is the defining equation of the golden ratio, and it appears here because the same quadratic governs any comparison between a self-overlapping pattern and a non-overlapping one. The comparison is genuinely two-sided: for a coin strongly biased towards heads ($p > 0.618$) the run $HH$ is the faster target, and for a fairer coin ($p < 0.618$) the mixed pattern $HT$ is faster, even though $HH$ is the more probable pattern for every $p > 1/2$.

The final comment is the part that cannot be answered by calculation alone. It is not enough to observe that 6 and 4 are different; the answer has to say what the difference is made of. The pattern probability is a red herring, and recognising which variable in a problem is a red herring -- rather than assuming that the most obvious quantity must be the governing one -- is the transferable skill.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 2.12 Cubic graphs: the three-real-root interval and the width of that interval
questions.question:
The figure shows part of the graph of $y = x^3 - 3x + 1$ together with three horizontal lines $y = a$.

Let $f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 1$ and consider the equation $f(x) = a$.

(a)

Find the coordinates of the two stationary points of $f$ and state the nature of each.

[3]

(b)

State the set of values of $a$ for which the equation $f(x) = a$ has three distinct real roots.

[2]

(c)

For $a$ in this set, let the three roots be $x_1 < x_2 < x_3$. Show that $x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 0$, that $x_1 x_3 = x_2^2 - 3$, and hence that $x_3 - x_1 = \sqrt{12 - 3x_2^2}$.

[5]

(d)

Hence find the greatest possible value of $x_3 - x_1$, and explain why this is larger than the value at either end of the range found in part (b).

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x-1)(x+1)$ (M1), so $f'(x) = 0$ at $x = \pm 1$. $f(-1) = -1 + 3 + 1 = 3$ and $f(1) = 1 - 3 + 1 = -1$ (A1). $f''(x) = 6x$, so $f''(-1) = -6 < 0$ and $(-1, 3)$ is a local maximum, while $f''(1) = 6 > 0$ and $(1, -1)$ is a local minimum (A1).

(b) Three distinct real roots occur exactly when the horizontal line $y = a$ cuts the curve between the two turning values, so $-1 < a < 3$ (A1)(A1) — the inequality is strict, since at $a = 3$ and at $a = -1$ two of the roots coincide.

(c) The equation $f(x) = a$ is $x^3 - 3x + 1 - a = 0$, a cubic with roots $x_1, x_2, x_3$. By Vieta, the sum of the roots is minus the coefficient of $x^2$, which is zero, so $x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 0$ (M1)(A1). The sum of pairwise products is the coefficient of $x$, so $x_1x_2 + x_2x_3 + x_3x_1 = -3$ (M1). Hence $x_2(x_1 + x_3) + x_1x_3 = -3$, and since $x_1 + x_3 = -x_2$ this gives $-x_2^2 + x_1x_3 = -3$, that is $x_1x_3 = x_2^2 - 3$ (A1). Finally $(x_3 - x_1)^2 = (x_1 + x_3)^2 - 4x_1x_3 = x_2^2 - 4(x_2^2 - 3) = 12 - 3x_2^2$ (M1), and $x_3 - x_1 > 0$, so $x_3 - x_1 = \sqrt{12 - 3x_2^2}$ (A1) (AG).

(d) $x_3 - x_1 = \sqrt{12 - 3x_2^2}$ is greatest when $x_2 = 0$ (M1), giving $x_3 - x_1 = \sqrt{12} = 2\sqrt3 \approx 3.46$ (A1). This exceeds $3$, the width at each end of the range: at $a = 3$ the roots are $-1$ (repeated) and $2$, and at $a = -1$ they are $-2$ and $1$ (repeated), so both extreme levels give a width of exactly $3$ (R1). The reason is that the width is governed by $x_2$, not by $a$: as $a$ moves away from the value that puts the middle root at the origin, $|x_2|$ grows and the width falls, so the ends of the parameter range give the narrowest intervals rather than the widest.
questions.explanation:
This is a parameter-range question wearing the clothes of a graph question, and the figure is there to make the wrong answer look right. Every candidate finds the turning values in (a) and the interval $-1 < a < 3$ in (b) without difficulty; the item is decided by (d).

The natural, and wrong, move is to assume the three roots are furthest apart when the horizontal line is as far as possible from the middle of the range — that is, at the two tangency levels $a = 3$ and $a = -1$, where one pair of roots has just merged. Both those levels give a width of exactly $3$. The truth is the opposite: the width is $\sqrt{12 - 3x_2^2}$, a function of the middle root alone, so it is largest when the middle root passes through the origin — at $a = 1$, in the centre of the range — where it is $2\sqrt3 \approx 3.46$.

The step that unlocks this is Vieta. The cubic is monic with no $x^2$ term, so the roots sum to zero and the quantity $x_3 - x_1$ can be rewritten entirely in terms of $x_2$; once that is done the maximisation is one line. Candidates who try to work with $a$ directly have no handle, because $a$ and $x_2$ are related by $x_2^3 - 3x_2 + 1 = a$, which cannot be inverted by hand. The second common error is to confuse the width with the difference of the outer roots computed at a single convenient value of $a$ and generalised from one case.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 5.11 The fundamental theorem applied across a point where the integrand does not exist
questions.question:
A student is asked to evaluate $\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{2} \frac{1}{x^{2}} \, dx$ and writes

$$\int_{-1}^{2} \frac{1}{x^{2}} \, dx = \left[ -\frac{1}{x} \right]_{-1}^{2}
= -\frac{1}{2} - \left(-\frac{1}{-1}\right) = -\frac{1}{2} - 1 = -\frac{3}{2}.$$

The graph of $y = \frac{1}{x^{2}}$ on $[-1, 2]$ is shown.

(a) Explain, without doing any integration, why the student's answer cannot be correct. \tag{3}

(b) Show that $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2} \frac{1}{x^{2}} \, dx$ does not converge. \tag{4}

(c) Explain what this implies about $\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{2} \frac{1}{x^{2}} \, dx$. \tag{3}

(d) Now let $a > 0$ and define $I(a) = \displaystyle \int_{-1}^{2} \frac{1}{x^{2} + a^{2}} \, dx$.
Find $I(a)$ in terms of $a$, and deduce that $I(a) \to \infty$ as $a \to 0^{+}$. \tag{3}

(a)

Explain, without integrating, why the student's answer cannot be correct.

[3]

(b)

Show that $\int_{0}^{2} \frac{1}{x^{2}} \, dx$ does not converge.

[4]

(c)

Explain what this implies about $\int_{-1}^{2} \frac{1}{x^{2}} \, dx$.

[3]

(d)

Find $I(a)$ in terms of $a$ and deduce that $I(a) \to \infty$ as $a \to 0^{+}$.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) On its domain, $\frac{1}{x^{2}} > 0$ for every $x \neq 0$ (A1). Wherever a definite
integral of a non-negative function exists it must be non-negative, being a limit of sums of
non-negative terms (R1). The student's value $-\frac{3}{2}$ is negative, so it cannot be the
value of the integral (A1). The figure makes the point visually: the curve never goes below
the axis, so no sensible notion of "area under the curve" can give $-1.5$.

(b) Treat the integral as an improper integral and integrate up to the singularity (M1):

$$\int_{\varepsilon}^{2} \frac{1}{x^{2}} \, dx = \left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_{\varepsilon}^{2}
= -\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\varepsilon}, \qquad \varepsilon > 0 \tag{A1}$$

As $\varepsilon \to 0^{+}$, $\frac{1}{\varepsilon} \to \infty$ (A1), so the limit does not
exist as a finite number and

$$\int_{0}^{2} \frac{1}{x^{2}} \, dx = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^{+}} \int_{\varepsilon}^{2}
\frac{1}{x^{2}} \, dx$$

diverges (AG). The divergence is not caused by the interval being long but by the integrand
being unbounded near a single point.

(c) The interval $[-1, 2]$ contains $x = 0$, at which the integrand is undefined (A1). An
integral over $[-1, 2]$ can only be defined by splitting at that point, as
$\int_{-1}^{0} + \int_{0}^{2}$, and each piece must converge separately for the whole to
converge (R1). Since the second piece diverges by part (b),
$\int_{-1}^{2} \frac{1}{x^{2}} \, dx$ does not converge and has no value at all — not
$-\frac{3}{2}$, not any other number (A1). The student's calculation smuggled a
discontinuous antiderivative across a point where the function it differentiates to does not
exist.

(d) For $a > 0$ the integrand is continuous everywhere, so the fundamental theorem applies
directly (M1):

$$I(a) = \left[ \frac{1}{a}\arctan\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) \right]_{-1}^{2}
= \frac{1}{a}\left(\arctan\left(\frac{2}{a}\right) + \arctan\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)\right)
\tag{A1}$$

As $a \to 0^{+}$, both $\frac{2}{a}$ and $\frac{1}{a}$ tend to $+\infty$, so both arctangents
tend to $\frac{\pi}{2}$ and their sum tends to $\pi$. Hence
$I(a) \sim \frac{\pi}{a} \to \infty$ as $a \to 0^{+}$ (AG). The parameter $a$ is a
regularisation: it removes the singularity at the cost of making the integral finite, and the
value blows up at exactly the rate one would expect as the regularisation is removed.
questions.explanation:
What makes this a good trap is that it can be caught before any analysis is done. The
integrand is positive; the answer is negative. That is a contradiction, and it is available to
a candidate who has not yet thought about improper integrals at all. Part (a) exists to hand
the candidate that observation, and everything afterwards is an explanation of it.

The student's error is a specific and common one. The fundamental theorem of calculus requires
the integrand to be continuous on the closed interval of integration. Here the interval
$[-1, 2]$ contains $x = 0$, where $\frac{1}{x^{2}}$ is not defined, and no amount of correct
antidifferentiation on either side repairs that. The function $-\frac{1}{x}$ differentiates to
$\frac{1}{x^{2}}$ on $(-\infty, 0)$ and on $(0, \infty)$ separately, and it is continuous
across $x = 0$ in no sense at all — it jumps from $+\infty$ to $-\infty$. Substituting the
endpoints into it computes something, but not the area under the curve.

Part (d) is the part that makes the item more than a cautionary tale. Replacing $x^{2}$ by
$x^{2} + a^{2}$ with $a > 0$ gives an integrand that is continuous on the whole real line, so
the fundamental theorem genuinely applies and $I(a)$ is finite for every $a$. Letting
$a \to 0^{+}$ recovers the original integrand pointwise but not in integral: the limit of the
integrals is infinite, and the rate, $\frac{\pi}{a}$, is the same $\frac{1}{a}$ blow-up that
appeared in part (b) when the lower limit $\varepsilon$ was sent to zero. The two calculations
are the same phenomenon seen from two directions, and seeing that is the real payoff.

There is a useful general lesson in the shape of the answer. When a computation returns a
value with the wrong sign, the wrong order of magnitude, or the wrong units, the fastest
diagnostic is almost never to redo the algebra — it is to ask whether the theorem being used
actually applies. Here the sign check takes about five seconds and rules out an entire
calculation.

questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.subtopic: 5.16 A definite integral that needs a substitution nobody has supplied, built by completing the square rather than recognised from a list, with an integrand whose obvious candidate fails
questions.question:
Define
$$I(a) = \int_{0}^{a} \frac{dx}{x^{2} + x + 1} \qquad \text{for } a > 0.$$

(a)

Show by completing the square that $x^{2} + x + 1 = \left(x + \dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} + \dfrac{3}{4}$, and hence that the substitution $u = \dfrac{2x + 1}{\sqrt{3}}$ turns the integrand into $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \cdot \dfrac{1}{1 + u^{2}}$.

[3]

(b)

Hence show that the limits $x = 0$ and $x = 1$ become $u = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ and $u = \sqrt{3}$, and evaluate $I(1)$ as an exact multiple of $\pi$.

[3]

(c)
